# OverlayController Export History

This record was originally meant to address just two terms in the compatibility closeout: OverlayController public export and polite validation feedback. Review found that the early description of the controller as an internal overlays object was too strong. That statement was only meant to say "no evidence of calls through the package entrypoint has been found yet," but it later became all too easy to read as "consumers should not access it." This revision retains the history behind that wording but no longer treats it as an interface decision.

## The Earlier Breakdown

The issue is still handled at three levels: the entrypoint, the instance, and the check results. At the entrypoint level, the goal is to find the constructor the package provides to consumers; at the instance level, lifecycle actions such as show and hide are discussed only after the constructor has been obtained; at the feedback level, run polite validation feedback once through the current public entrypoint and record what that execution actually returns or throws.

These three levels cannot answer for one another. A local test's ability to create an object does not mean consumers can obtain the constructor from the package entrypoint. A lack of recorded validation output does not mean there is no feedback at runtime. Conversely, seeing a feedback result does not establish that OverlayController is exported.

## Options Considered During Review

There were three options at the time.

First, state directly in the compatibility notes that the controller is public, then verify the entrypoint later. Not adopted. Callers would integrate based on the notes first; if the entrypoint name or access method turned out to differ, adding evidence later would mean retracting integration guidance that had already circulated.

Second, remove public export and retain only the description of it as an internal overlays object. Also not adopted. public export is exactly what needs to be checked in this round. Removing the term would not eliminate the requirement; it would only remove a stable reference point for later searches.

Third, keep public export as a target to be confirmed, while recording the package entrypoint, constructor, and instance actions separately. The third option was adopted. It allows the interface review to continue without turning an observation from a local test directly into a consumer contract.

polite validation feedback is treated with the same restraint. It remains a separate execution item and is not closed out early because of progress on the controller. Without actual output, the record can only say "returned or thrown content still to be added"; it cannot be filled in with an invented success message, exception text, or browser behavior.

## Reframing the Search Path

The earlier investigation always started from `packages/overlays/test/LocalOverlayController.test.js`. It is a useful navigation point because the filename matches LocalOverlayController, and the file header also lists the dependencies needed for local tests:

```js
import { expect, fixture, html, aTimeout, defineCE, unsafeStatic } from '@open-wc/testing';
import Popper from 'popper.js/dist/esm/popper.min.js';
import { keyCodes } from '../src/utils/key-codes.js';
import { simulateTab } from '../src/utils/simulate-tab.js';
```

But this path cannot provide all the evidence needed to establish the package entrypoint. `fixture`, `html`, `defineCE`, and `unsafeStatic` show how the tests prepare elements; Popper is a positioning dependency in the surrounding test context; `keyCodes` and `simulateTab` show that the local scenarios also examine keyboard and focus paths. They do not turn the test file into a package export, nor do they automatically show how consumers obtain the constructor.

Only half of the old search sequence is therefore retained: the test file can be a starting point for understanding the object's context, but once the object is found, the investigation must return to the package entrypoint. If the entrypoint has been confirmed, then observe show and hide on an instance that has been obtained; if the issue is feedback wording or timing, use polite validation's public check entrypoint instead. Collapsing all three into "the controller is usable" makes it impossible, when something fails, to tell whether the problem is with the export, the instance, or the feedback record.

**The earlier "treat as an internal object" label has been retired.** It remains in the history because it did affect the investigation order; it no longer indicates that the object is internal, nor does it mean that a public export does not exist. DOC-12 continue to cover pre-attachment event delegation and validator factory compatibility; this page does not use those two items as a substitute for its own entrypoint assessment.

## What Remains Open

This revision still has no samples from real callers and no saved record of what polite validation feedback actually returned or threw. These gaps are not a negative finding. Follow-up review needs to leave two separate kinds of evidence: one showing which package entrypoint consumers use to obtain the constructor, and the other showing what was observed after running validation through the public entrypoint.

Although both tasks belong to the 2019.11 compatibility closeout, they do not share a source location or a failure symptom. If validation results arrive first, they cannot be used as grounds to skip the controller's entrypoint check; if the controller's entrypoint is confirmed, that cannot be used to fill in validation's feedback results either. The decision is to retain public export as an investigation target, use the entrypoint—constructor—instance actions breakdown, and keep polite validation feedback as a separate execution record awaiting completion.

# OverlayController Export History

This page was not written in one sitting as an interface specification. It started with two adjacent compatibility terms, then was repeatedly rewritten in response to test paths, a check that was never closed out, and follow-up questions from users. The earliest record left two questions: "whether to make it public" and "whether the feedback had been confirmed"; intermediate versions tried to organize them into several items that could be checked separately; only in the most recent review were the interface relationships that could now be settled separated from the feedback issues for which runtime results still needed to be retained.

The old paragraphs remain below. They were not retroactively rewritten to match today's correct account, because the misreadings at the time had changed the search order. Sentences marked "deprecated" can explain why this page took its current form, but can no longer serve as a basis for integration.

## 4 2023: The Two Threads Were Initially Kept Side by Side

The initial note left only two phrases: OverlayController public export, polite validation feedback. There was no call example naming the package entrypoint, nor any returned text from validation feedback. At the time, the person keeping the record was unwilling to describe an interface as already public without evidence, so they initially placed controller in the context of internal collaboration within overlays and left feedback as another check still to be performed.

This framing served a purpose at the time. Wrapping up compatibility work required someone to first pin down the object names, to keep the discussion from drifting from OverlayController to the entire overlay lifecycle; it was also necessary to prevent callers from integrating directly based on a line of text that had not yet been reviewed. The early record therefore split the issue into three layers: whether users could obtain the constructor, whether they could use show and hide after obtaining an instance, and what feedback the public check entrypoint actually left.

But the note contained a statement that was easy to misread: until there is a package entrypoint call example, treat it as an internal object for now. It was only intended to express "not announcing it yet", not "confirmed as internal". These two meanings were not distinguished in writing at the time, so someone later inferred the package's public boundary from local objects in test files. That judgment is retained in this version as a record of the earlier state, and can no longer be treated as a decision.

The early material contained neither actual callers nor validation output. Without these, neither the way to obtain the constructor nor feedback messages, exceptions, or display order can be filled in. What the initial record really left was only a working distinction: entrypoints and instance actions must not be conflated, and the controller's name cannot stand in for feedback.

## 12 2023: Review Downgrades "Internal" Back to a Working Hypothesis

The second revision did not delete the early note. The review addendum first changed how it should be read: the old "internal object" label meant only that the entrypoint relationship had not yet been reviewed, and could not express the user-facing contract. This small correction mattered, because it retained the caution while removing the mistaken classification.

What was on the table at the time was not a complete comparison of technical implementations, but which kind of risk the record should take on.

One approach is to first state in the compatibility notes that controller is already available for consumers to integrate with, then look for the package entrypoint afterward. Supporters of this approach believe that callers only need a clear conclusion; the objection is that once an entry point that has not been rechecked is treated as an integration point, even if the actual relationship is identified later, it will still be necessary to explain why the earlier notes can no longer be used.

The second approach is to remove public export from the record and continue maintaining the record based only on internal objects. It appears to reduce uncertainty, but in fact it merely erases the subject of this round of investigation. Since the requirements history has already explicitly named public export, deleting the term cannot resolve the entry point issue.

The third approach is to retain public export, but record package entrypoint, constructor, and instance actions separately. This approach was adopted. It does not require a single local file to establish all the interfaces at once, nor does it allow a single observation from a test to stand in for the entire consumer contract.

polite validation feedback is still not included in this decision. The check for it is to run it once through the current public entry point and save what is actually returned or thrown. There was no complete output at the time, so the gap must remain, and it cannot be described as "no feedback". This also meant that the two topics on the same page progressed toward closure at different rates: the interface hierarchy for controller could be clarified first, while feedback still needed its own runtime evidence.

## Test file: the entry point is nearby, but the export is not here

The lookup path that has long been retained is:

`packages/overlays/test/LocalOverlayController.test.js`

The earlier investigation used the issue and call names to get here. The path itself is not wrong, as it can lead readers to the tests surrounding LocalOverlayController, avoiding an aimless search of the entire repository. The mistake came after stopping here: someone saw that the tests could set up and manipulate local objects and wrote this up as consumers already having access to the package constructor.

The following direct dependencies can be seen at the top of the file:

```js
import { expect, fixture, html, aTimeout, defineCE, unsafeStatic } from '@open-wc/testing';
import Popper from 'popper.js/dist/esm/popper.min.js';
import { keyCodes } from '../src/utils/key-codes.js';
import { simulateTab } from '../src/utils/simulate-tab.js';
```

These names show the scope of the test environment. `@open-wc/testing` provides assertions, fixture support, HTML snippets, waiting, and custom element setup; Popper appears alongside the tests for overlay positioning; `keyCodes` and `simulateTab` allow keyboard- and focus-related scenarios to be reproduced in tests. They can help explain why the file kept being opened during the earlier investigation, but the import list cannot be used to infer the public-facing relationships of the overlays package entrypoint.

### The old path that was retained

Earlier records treated "finding the controller through `LocalOverlayController.test.js`" as sufficient evidence that the public export had been confirmed. This conclusion is now marked as deprecated. The test file remains a starting point for tracing back, and the fixture and element setup in the tests are still useful; what has been deprecated is its status as a criterion for the package export, not the file itself.

When continuing along this path, first identify which object the local test is operating on, then return separately to the package entrypoint to check the consumer-facing entry point. Only after obtaining the constructor should you move on to the instance lifecycle; if the field report only mentions abnormal feedback, trace the public check entry point directly, without using object construction in the test file to supply an execution result for it.

## A Field Note That Was Never Closed Out

At one point, a check attempted to close out both lines of inquiry at once: the local test could construct the controller, so the controller was provisionally considered usable; validation had not yet produced any output, so it was not pursued further for the time being. This did not become a formal decision, but it was retained in the material because it shows how "the object can be created" and "the consumer can obtain it" were conflated.

This approach had two specific problems. First, object availability in the test context only shows that the context can prepare the object, not that the caller can obtain the constructor from the package entry point. Second, failing to save what validation returned or threw only shows that the record from that check was incomplete, not that the feedback path did not run, much less that the feedback functionality does not exist.

The combined status was later split up. On the OverlayController side, only three questions were investigated: whether the package entrypoint is public, whether the constructor can be obtained, and whether show and hide can be called after obtaining an instance. On the polite validation feedback side, only the actual result of one execution through the public entry point was saved. This did not make the material complete, but it prevented the word "usable" from covering exports, instances, and feedback all at once.

This field note also explains why the validation text was not moved into the overlays test notes. The two items being adjacent in the same compatibility train does not mean they share a source code location, failure symptoms, or a method of proof. They were kept on one page to preserve their historical relationship; they were separated so that one object would not answer questions on behalf of the other.

## Review Notes: An Adjacent Issue Cannot Substitute for This Decision

The correction left by subsequent reviews was: until the entry point has been checked, do not assume on the consumer's behalf that the controller is internal, and do not prematurely claim that it is already public. This correction did not remove the old label, because the old label had actually affected the investigation; it merely demoted the label from a decision to a historical trace.

The review also kept several easily conflated subjects separate. pre-attachment event delegation is a related issue in the interface review, and validator factory compatibility is also covered by DOC-12. They may come up in the same round of compatibility discussions, but no material shows that they can provide evidence for the export of OverlayController or replace the execution records for polite validation feedback. The presence of DOC-12 only provides navigation, without changing the scope of the decision on this page.

Three terms recur in the meeting side notes: package entrypoint, constructor, and feedback output. The full sequence of remarks was not preserved, nor were the side notes organized into a voting table. These three terms were later interpreted as two distinct branches: the first two concerned interface relationships, and the last concerned runtime records. The side notes are kept brief here because they show where the review actually got stuck, not to add a generic methodology to the current decision.

During the review, there was also disagreement over whether to combine the constructor and instance actions into a single statement, "controller is usable". Those in favor of combining them looked only at the call results, while those in favor of keeping them separate pointed out that entrypoint failures and instance method failures would lead back to different places. In the end, they remained separate. For this subject, entrypoint changes, obtaining the constructor, and instance action failures are not the same kind of issue; combining them into one statement would recreate the original misreading.

## 2025: Two cards route the gaps to different entrypoints

Only later materials introduced two trackable work items. The local description for LION-201 calls for finding the actual call behind the most recent report of "OverlayController public export" and adding back how it was called and what the user saw. It supplies the caller walkthrough that had remained unavailable in the early stages: moving from names and test adjacency to actual usage locations.

In later activity, LION-201 first recorded a caller walkthrough, then moved from To Do to In Progress. What can be confirmed here is the direction of the work and the status change, not a particular caller, page, or result inferred from the card's name. If a call sample is to be included on this page, it must still retain its own calling context; an imagined user scenario cannot be used to fill the gap.

LION-218 is responsible for confirming the execution of the existing polite validation checks. Its local requirement is to run "polite validation feedback" through the current public entrypoint, recording only what this path actually returns or throws. The item was later completed after being In Progress, but the frozen material on this page does not provide output text, a message format or an exception type. The completion action therefore only shows that this work was handled, and cannot be stretched to mean that any particular feedback content has been proven on this page.

The two cards serve only as navigation aids here. LION-201 points to the gap at the caller entrypoint, while LION-218 points to the gap in validation execution. They cannot jointly constitute proof of compatibility, nor can they let readers skip over the two distinct levels of entrypoint and instance. Still less can work items created only in 2025 be retroactively treated as facts already known in 2023.

This time gap is part of the history. Although the early discussions already used the term public export, they had no caller walkthrough, with actual calls only later listed as an explicit follow-up investigation task. Separate confirmation of validation execution also did not come until even later. The gaps in the older version are therefore accurate, not omissions of material that only appeared later.

## Current Interface Decision

Following the breakdown above, the current interface statement is: The overlays package entrypoint publicly exports the OverlayController constructor, and an instance exposes callable show() and hide() lifecycle methods.

This sentence covers only the overlays package entrypoint, the OverlayController constructor, and the `show()` and `hide()` lifecycle methods on an instance obtained from the constructor. It does not extend to Popper's positioning behavior, does not describe how the LocalOverlayController test fixture constructs elements, and does not specify returned text, display timing or an exception form for polite validation feedback.

The interface relationships can be read along this local path:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PackageEntrypoint
    PackageEntrypoint --> OverlayControllerConstructor
    OverlayControllerConstructor --> Instance
    Instance --> ShowHideMethods
    PackageEntrypoint --> PoliteValidationFeedback
    ShowHideMethods --> [*]
    PoliteValidationFeedback --> [*]
```

For callers, the starting point for lookup is the overlays package entrypoint, not the local construction pattern in a test file. After obtaining the constructor, verify show() and hide() on the instance; if the problem is at the entrypoint, do not jump directly to instance methods, and if the problem is with the instance, do not infer that the entrypoint does not exist. The old "treat it as an internal object" approach no longer applies within this scope.

This decision does not add polite validation feedback to the lifecycle contract of OverlayController. They still appear on the same page because they once jointly blocked compatibility finalization, and because the history needs to preserve their original side-by-side relationship. The feedback content should still come from the actual returned or thrown result obtained through the public check entrypoint indicated by LION-218, rather than be inferred from the controller's public status.

## feedback remains a separate line of verification

The current documentation scope for polite validation feedback is very narrow: execute through the public entrypoint and retain the content actually returned or thrown. The frozen materials do not contain that content, so this page does not document success messages, failure text, or behavior guaranteed to occur in a particular browser. Completing LION-218 did not change this factual boundary.

There are two opposite misconceptions to avoid when investigating. Seeing that the controller already has a clearly defined interface does not mean validation output can be omitted; seeing that the validation work item is complete does not mean the package entrypoint can be skipped. If both types of symptoms appear in the same case, retain the entrypoint or instance observations and the actual validation output separately. Their shared context is compatibility finalization, not a shared runtime conclusion.

This is also why this page does not reproduce the proposal content from DOC-12. pre-attachment event delegation, validator factory compatibility, and feedback checks may appear alongside one another in release reviews, but this page only documents their boundaries: they cannot serve as substitute evidence for the OverlayController public export, nor can they replace a validation run. The full interface comparison remains in the materials to which DOC-12 belong.

## Older test-adjacent examples

`packages/overlays/test/LocalOverlayController.test.js` is still worth keeping in the navigation. The direct dependencies in the file clearly define the test setup:`@open-wc/testing` handles `expect`,`fixture`,`html`,`aTimeout`,`defineCE`,`unsafeStatic`; Popper comes from `popper.js/dist/esm/popper.min.js`; keyboard and focus scenarios also use `keyCodes` and `simulateTab`.

These objects show that the reader is entering a local test environment, not a declaration page for the package entrypoint. The test file can help trace the elements, positioning, waiting and focus behavior around LocalOverlayController; when the question becomes how consumers obtain the constructor, it is still necessary to return to the package entrypoint. Listing imports as public exports would mistake test utilities for consumer dependencies, and would also mistake an easily accessible file for the definitive location of the definition.

### Old example A: Stopping at the test file

The old record recommended: first open the tests for LocalOverlayController, and after seeing controller-related objects, mark the public export as confirmed. This recommendation was later abandoned, but was not deleted. It explains why early investigations always started with the same file, and also explains how the misjudgment arose: the file name, issue name and name used in the call were similar, and the test fixtures could quickly produce an object that could be operated on.

The only part that can now be retained is "enter the local context from here". What cannot be retained is "stopping here is enough to prove the package exports". If someone follows the old path in the future, the test objects, package entrypoint and way consumers obtain the constructor should be documented as three distinct observation points, rather than treating file location as interface ownership.

### Old example B: Treating no output as no feedback

Another old claim was that no return content had been written down for polite validation feedback, so it should initially be treated as having no feedback. That claim was later overturned. Missing output means the material was not saved, and does not directly indicate whether there was feedback at runtime. This example also remains on record, because it distinguishes between the two gaps of "entrypoint relationships not verified" and "execution results not recorded".

These two gaps require different approaches: for the former, return to the package entrypoint and caller walkthrough, and for the latter, use the public check entrypoint to save what is returned or thrown. They can occur together, or only one may occur; labeling both as "unsupported" would prevent later readers from determining where to return.

## Boundaries not yet separated out

caller walkthrough still needs to retain the result visible to the user, while this page's interface decision covers only the package entrypoint, constructor, and instance lifecycle methods. If specific call scenarios are filled in later, they should remain in the context of the caller-facing material and should not insert a user from some page or a hypothetical user here.

Dependencies in test files also belong only to the test adjacency. Popper, key codes, tab simulation, and Open WC test tools can help pinpoint local scenarios, but they have not been frozen as public exports. If tracing back from the test files, we still need to distinguish between "being able to construct an object in the test context" and "the user obtaining the constructor from the package entrypoint."

This page ultimately records two distinct conclusion states. The entrypoint and instance lifecycle of OverlayController have already been clearly decided at the interface level; the behavior of polite validation feedback must still be based on what is actually returned or thrown. Old internal labels, the claim that test files themselves are exports, and the claim that no output means no feedback all remain in the historical record, but they can only serve as explanations and are no longer a basis for new judgments.

# Pre-Mount Event Delegation Proposal

This proposal grew out of two adjacent issues during the compatibility closeout for 2019.11: whether callers can register events before the overlay content appears, and whether the current API can still handle the validator factory's legacy calling convention. Both involve public APIs, but they are not being treated as the same implementation change yet.

There are two initial paths: keep a delegation entry point in the controller so later-created content remains covered by the listener, or require callers to wait until the content is created before binding directly. The former is friendlier to legacy callers; the latter has a smaller implementation footprint but changes the registration timing. For the validator factory, leave open whether the compatibility layer belongs inside the factory or on the caller side.

The review entry point is `packages/overlays/test/LocalOverlayController.test.js`. The file already shows `@open-wc/testing`'s fixture utilities, Popper, key codes, and tab simulation helpers. First add a test that registers a listener during construction, then add a sample of the factory's legacy invocation. # Pre-mount Event Delegation Proposal

The previous version tied the two issues too closely together: it made it sound as though delaying listener registration until after content creation would resolve both compatibility concerns. After reviewing them, we're separating them first. Event delegation concerns the relative timing of controller and content creation when a listener is registered; the validator factory concerns whether legacy factory calls still produce a usable validator. They can be checked in the same round, but should not share a single compatibility decision.

`packages/overlays/test/LocalOverlayController.test.js` is still the test file we can work from directly. The dependencies at the top of the file include `fixture`, `html`, `aTimeout`, `defineCE`, and `unsafeStatic`, along with Popper, `keyCodes`, and `simulateTab`. These tools are enough to cover construction, mounting, keyboard actions, and asynchronous updates, but the file itself cannot determine what guarantees the public interface should provide.

There are two candidate approaches for event delegation. Approach A prepares a stable forwarding point when the controller is created and keeps using the same entry point once content appears. The advantage is that legacy callers do not need to know when content is created; the cost is that we need to verify how the forwarding point behaves on destruction, content replacement, and repeated registration. Approach B binds native listeners only after content exists. The implementation is more straightforward, but it requires callers to change their call order and may cause registrations during construction to fail silently. We're leaning toward A, but haven't yet committed to the behavior for destruction and repeated registration.

An adapter layer is a separate candidate for the validator factory. We can have the factory accept the old arguments and convert them at the boundary, or retain the strict new shape and migrate legacy callers to the new entry point. The former avoids a migration; the latter makes errors easier to catch. The cost of each depends on the old shape and the current return value, and the supplied material does not include the full signature. We won't invent parameter names here. The only examples needed are: a legacy call, a current call, and how the returned validator plugs into the existing validation flow.

Start by writing tests in observation order, without treating an undecided approach as a pass condition: register a listener during controller construction, then create content; next, register a second listener while content already exists; trigger events in each case and record which listener receives the callback. Then cover content replacement and controller cleanup. For the factory, only compare whether legacy and current calls can enter the same validation path; do not infer factory compatibility from the event tests.

If A leaves listeners behind during cleanup or content replacement, roll back the delegation forwarding implementation, not the regression tests we've added. If the old factory shape cannot be converted safely, do not present migration as compatibility support; leave the question open. Two points still need confirmation from the public interface owner: whether the delegation entry point is part of the public constructor's contract, and how broadly the validator factory's old shape needs to be supported.

# Pre-mount event delegation proposal

## Where this revision changes the boundary

The early draft treated "content has not been mounted yet" as a window that callers had to avoid, so option A was only a preferred implementation direction. The second version rechecked `packages/overlays/test/LocalOverlayController.test.js`, but only added the inspection entry points and candidate paths, without enough material to support this restriction. Recent feedback asks us to correct the timing assessment before discussing the legacy shape of the validator factory; the two compatibility tracks remain separate.

One claim here can easily be skewed by the old paragraphs: listeners only make sense once content exists. This is no longer retained as a premise of the proposal. The interface position now adopted is:

> An overlay controller exposes delegated addEventListener behavior before any content is attached, so listeners registered during construction remain effective.

This statement only addresses registration timing; it does not automatically determine the details of content replacement, destruction, or factory parameters. The proposal also does not extend "events can be received" into "all overlay lifecycles are now compatible".

## Trade-offs for the delegation entry point

Keeping a delegation entry point available during construction is the more worthwhile path to try in this round. Call Fang Ke to register `addEventListener` immediately after obtaining the controller, without waiting for the internal content to be created. Once content is created, events still need to reach the registered listeners through the forwarding relationship exposed by the controller. This preserves the old call order; the added cost is that the forwarding relationship must have a clearly defined lifetime.

The other path is to defer listener binding until after content is created. It does not require maintaining an early entry point, the code appears more narrowly scoped, and focused tests are easier to pass. However, this would expose the internal DOM timing to callers: registrations already completed during construction would have no natural handoff point. Unless the compatibility goal explicitly allows callers to change the order, this will not be the default proposal, and will remain only a fallback candidate if the delegation implementation cannot meet cleanup semantics.

Before implementation, first check four specific behaviors rather than expanding the public contract:

- After registration during construction, whether events still pass through the same forwarding point when content is first created;
- When content is replaced, whether listeners on the old node fire multiple times or remain active;
- After the controller is cleaned up, whether both the forwarding point and the content nodes stop operating;
- When the same event type is registered repeatedly, whether callers can remove their own listeners in the original way.

These four items define the scope of checks for the delegation candidate, not a finalized behavior matrix. The available material only supports treating the first item as a compatibility scenario that must be verified; the other three need to be settled based on the implementation results.

## Keep validator factory changes separate

"validator factory compatibility" is a related interface issue in this round. The old proposal placed it after event delegation, which could easily suggest that reusing the controller's adapter layer was all that was needed. The approach now is to retain call examples separately: the legacy factory call, the current factory call, and the points where their respective return values feed into validation feedback. The input does not include complete function signatures, parameter names, or returned-object fields, so API will not be filled in based on experience.

Candidate one supports legacy calls at the factory boundary, keeping conversion inside the factory. The benefit is a smaller migration footprint for callers; the risk is that once legacy parameters are silently accepted, errors may not surface until the validator is used. Candidate two maintains the strict shape of the current entry point and puts a short-term adapter on the caller side. The benefit is a clear point of failure; the cost is that every caller still using the old shape has to change. Candidate three only records the old shape and makes no commitment to runtime compatibility for now, which is appropriate when examples are insufficient but leaves the migration work to a later version.

At present, the overlay test file does not establish which candidate should be implemented. That file can host construction and event tests for delegation, and can also provide fixtures for the factory's integration into the validation flow; it is not a source for the legacy factory signature. The validator portion remains undecided until actual call examples are received, and a passing event test will not be used to declare both compatible.

## Experiment sequence

First, run a minimal construction-timing check: create a controller, immediately register a `addEventListener`, then make content appear and trigger the target event. Record whether the callback runs and whether it runs exactly once. Then use registration when content already exists as a control, to avoid mistaking "late registration works" for "early registration also works". The existing `fixture`, `html`, `aTimeout`, `defineCE`, `unsafeStatic` in the tests can be used as needed; retain Popper, `keyCodes`, `simulateTab` only when the corresponding specific behavior is actually being tested, and do not expand the proposal just because the file already has an import.

Only in the second step should content replacement and cleanup be examined. Record the listener registered before replacement, the events generated by the new node after replacement, and any residual callbacks after cleanup separately, and do not combine the three into one overall assertion. If a failure occurs, state only whether it occurs in timing, replacement, or cleanup, and do not infer the validator factory outcome from it.

In the third step, prepare the two factory call examples. Each example needs to retain the input shape, the returned result, and the step where it feeds into validation feedback; without these specific materials, only record TODO, and do not write "the legacy version is supported". If the old shape can be converted at the boundary, initially limit the work to an adapter-layer experiment; if conversion would swallow parameter errors, stop expanding the compatibility scope and switch to a caller migration plan.

## Rollback and open items

The rollback triggers for the delegation proposal are an inability to preserve cleanup semantics, or registrations made during construction failing to receive events reliably once the actual content appears. When rolling back, remove the newly added forwarding implementation and retain the tests that reproduce the problem, without recasting the failure as caller misuse. The rollback trigger for the validator factory is an inability to distinguish errors in legacy parameters from valid empty values; in that case, do not add permissive branches, and retain the migration candidate for now.

The following still need to be confirmed: whether the public constructor is the object from which callers obtain the delegation entry point; which layer is responsible for the lifecycle of content replacement; what the legacy call examples and current return values of the validator factory are. Until these three items are confirmed, only the event registration timing experiment can be approved, not a full factory compatibility claim.

# Global overlay content troubleshooting tree

First, a note on the global mask. The observed issue isn't that the mask never opens at all. It's that, when the caller-provided content is still visible on the page, the page output alone doesn't tell us what state the node the caller originally saved is in. For now, treat this as "global mode takes over the content"—a working assumption to continue the investigation, not a conclusion about node relationships.

Don't change the controller yet. Start observing after the fixture in `packages/overlays/test/DynamicGlobalLocal.test.js`. The file contains `DynamicOverlayController`, `GlobalOverlayController`, and `LocalOverlayController` next to each other. Having the names in the same test file doesn't mean the three modes are interchangeable for verification.

```text
Global mask content looks wrong
├─ Can't find the supplied content after the fixture
│  └─ Go back to the input side and first confirm the content was actually passed to the mask
├─ No visible content on the page
│  └─ Stay on the display side and check the global container first
├─ Content is visible on the page, but node relationships are unclear
│  └─ Record the caller's object and the page-side object
└─ Only the final text is available
   └─ Don't draw a conclusion about content identity yet
```

This entry point uses what `@open-wc/testing` provides: `expect`, `html`, and `fixture`. For this pass, just use the fixture to establish whether the content exists and where it is. If local mode behaves normally, record that only as a local-mode result; keep dynamic-mode results separate as well.

Retain US validator message extension as an adjacent observation at this stage. Save one visible result from a successful call and one from a failed call. Compare the text only when both produce feedback; if only one does, first check whether the other reaches the corresponding validator. Without results from both, don't guess at the internal cause from the final message.

Stop when you can clearly document the supplied content, the content visible on the page, and the location of the class separately, or when you've confirmed that the content is already missing before the fixture. In the latter case, go back to the caller; in the former, continue investigating the global container.

# Global Overlay Content Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally grouped two nearby symptoms: the relationships between content nodes were unclear after the global mask opened, and the visible feedback from the US validator message extension needed another check. Both came up around the compatibility wrap-up. That only means the investigation entry points were adjacent at the time, not that the two shared an internal cause.

The earliest wording was "Global mode takes over the content." This can help with initial triage: if the passed-in content never reached the fixture, don't start by explaining it in terms of styles and containers; if the page already has content, that at least confirms the display side isn't completely empty. But visible content on the page does not, by itself, tell us whether the object supplied by the caller is the object the display side is using. Matching text is not enough to establish object identity either.

The old triage branches remain, but their endpoints are narrower:

```text
After the global mask opens
├─ No passed-in content after the fixture
│  └─ Go back to the side that constructs the content; don't infer a cause from class in this pass
├─ No visible content on the page
│  └─ Check the display side first, then decide whether to continue
├─ The page has content
│  └─ Don't write "The content has not changed"; continue checking the object relationship
└─ Only a screenshot or the final text remains
   └─ Add fixture observations before making a judgment
```

The test entry point is still `packages/overlays/test/DynamicGlobalLocal.test.js`. It imports `DynamicOverlayController`, `GlobalOverlayController`, `LocalOverlayController`, as well as `@open-wc/testing`'s `expect`, `html`, and `fixture`. This shows where fixture observation starts. It does not define the container structures of the three controllers, and a passing local path does not justify closing out the global path.

During review, document "content" in three distinct places. The first is the content object handed over by the caller; the second is the content object accessible on the mask side; the third is the node carrying the global class. The first two are used to check the object relationship. The third is only used to check where the styling marker is applied. Calling all three "content" makes it easy to conflate node identity with visual state in the next pass.

```text
Some objects have been obtained
├─ Both the caller's object and the mask-side object are available
│  ├─ Compare whether they are the same object
│  └─ Record the actual location of the global class separately
├─ Only the caller's object is available
│  └─ Add mask-side observations; don't speculate about wrapping or replacement
├─ Only the mask-side object is available
│  └─ Go back and confirm whether the caller still holds the passed-in content
└─ Only text remains on both sides
   └─ Stop assigning object-level causes
```

One quick review checked only two things: the final text was still present, and there was a class near the global container. The old record therefore said "The content has not changed." That conclusion is withdrawn, but those two observations do not need to be withdrawn. The text can still show what the user saw, and the class can still help identify omissions on the display side. The problem is that neither observation retained the two objects or established whether the class was on the passed-in content, the container, or another display node.

So "content is visible and the class is present" can only be recorded as a result of the visual branch. When content is not visible, the investigation can stay with the container or display path first; when content is visible but the class is missing, record where it is missing; when content is visible and the class is present, the caller's object and the mask-side object must still be obtained. Visual results alone cannot establish "the object was replaced," "the object was moved," or "the object remained unchanged" as facts.

The review addendum also calls for an explicit endpoint for "the two objects are different." The old notes only asked whether the passed-in content had disappeared, and tended to stop once text was still visible on the page. Now, if the caller still holds the original object while the mask side provides a different object for inspection, retain both in the record and mark the class location separately. Different objects are just an observation; without evidence from before and after attachment, do not go on to attribute it to deletion, rewriting, or destruction.

The US validator message extension remains a separate adjacent check. Do not use the global mask's object branches to explain the messages here. First separate successful calls from failed calls:

```text
US validator message extension
├─ Both success and failure have visible feedback
│  └─ Record the text and where it appears for each
├─ Only one has visible feedback
│  └─ First confirm whether the other reaches the corresponding validator
├─ Neither has visible feedback
│  └─ Stop at call observation
└─ Only the final error text remains
   └─ Add one set of results for success and one for failure
```

The old notes recommended comparing the final error wording directly. That is still useful once feedback has been confirmed on both sides, but it does not cover "no feedback" or "the call did not reach the validator." Differences in message text cannot, in turn, prove the content relationship in the global mask.

Bring back two kinds of evidence for the next review: the two content objects and the location of the global class in the global path; and the visible results of two calls, one successful and one failed, in the message path. If the symptom occurs only in local mode, this page's global branch ends here.

# Global Overlay Content Troubleshooting Tree

This page has remained in the compatibility closeout materials for a long time. Initially it contained only a few lines recording where the global mask content went, and later notes on visible feedback issues with the US validator message extension were added alongside them. The two topics have never been separated, not because a shared implementation had already been found, but because reviews at the time often started from the same set of test entry points, and regression notes had already referenced the old records.

The part still worth preserving is the initial triage: first distinguish between content that never entered the fixture and content that has already appeared on the page, but whose object relationships were not recorded. The early conclusions can no longer be used directly for closeout. The following sections are arranged in the order recorded in the supplementary notes, with the old wording retained in its original position and the parts that are no longer valid marked where needed.

## 2023-03-20: The initial global mask notes

The first symptom observed was: after opening the global mask, the page could still display content, but the node retained by the caller could not be verified from the page output alone. The first draft condensed this into the single phrase "global mode takes over the content". At the time only the visible result was examined, the passed-in object and the display-side object were not recorded together, and no one asked which node the class actually ended up on.

The steps taken at the time were brief. Leave the controller unchanged for now, and first check the content after fixture. The entry point was written as `packages/overlays/test/DynamicGlobalLocal.test.js`. The file showed `DynamicOverlayController`,`GlobalOverlayController` and `LocalOverlayController` next to each other, so the first draft included a reminder not to collapse the three names dynamic, local, and global into a single behavior. That reminder is still valid; the explanation of "taking over the content" is no longer sufficient.

```text
Initial triage
├─ No passed-in content after fixture
│  └─ Return to where the caller constructs the content
├─ Content is present after fixture, but absent from the page
│  └─ Stay on the global display side
└─ Content is still present on the page
   └─ Written at the time as "content has been taken over"
```

The last line is the old working interpretation. Its only purpose at the time was to prompt further inspection around the container, not to serve as evidence of object identity. The presence of content on the page shows at most that the display is not completely blank; it cannot establish whether the node handed over by the caller was used directly, nor what the caller still holds.

The first draft did not make "content is present on the page but the objects differ" a separate branch. That was a distinction easily missed in each subsequent review: the text can be identical while the two nodes may still be different; likewise, the presence of a styled node on the page does not mean that the style is on the node passed in by the caller.

## Same-day side note: what to record first after fixture

The test entry point uses `@open-wc/testing`, and the visible imports include `expect`, `html`, and `fixture`. The old side notes did not explain the internal behavior of these tools, but only used the point after the fixture for observation. If the content is already absent before the fixture, continuing to compare the class or the final DOM text is not helpful; only if the content has reached the fixture is it necessary to continue distinguishing between the caller-side object, the mask-side object, and the display-side styles.

The side notes were originally written as three lines and have been kept ever since:

```text
When the page already has content, also record:
- whether the caller can still retrieve the content object it handed over;
- which content object is actually received at the mask check;
- the exact node where the global class is observed.
```

This is not a diagram of implementation steps, nor does it mean that the controller necessarily has three fixed internal stages. It is only meant to prevent someone from coming back with nothing but screenshots next time. In particular, the third line must not just say "there is a class near the container" and stop there: that wording cannot distinguish whether the class is on the passed-in content, the outer container, or another node used for display.

The early side notes also listed local mode and dynamic mode alongside this. They exist in the same test entry point and can only serve as nearby navigation aids. When the local result is normal, the record can say "the local path is normal"; this statement must not be extended to mean that the identity of the content on the global path has been confirmed. The same applies to the dynamic path, and unless the actual observation is already in dynamic mode, do not use it to answer questions on behalf of the global branch.

## Brief message-side notes left in 2023

US validator message extension was added during the same phase. The initial material was insufficient to establish which layer produced the message, or to infer the validator's behavior from a single final message text. Therefore, the old record only required saving the visible results of one successful call and one failed call separately.

The narrow rule at the time was: when both sides have messages, compare the text; without material from both sides, do not guess at the locale, factory, or internal validator path. This rule deliberately kept message issues out of the mask branch. The fact that both involve visible content does not mean that the global container, content wrapping, and validation feedback are related.

```text
Old message record
├─ Both calls have feedback
│  └─ Record the text displayed by each
├─ Only one call has feedback
│  └─ Add the result of the other call
└─ No visible feedback
   └─ Do not infer the cause from the wording yet
```

This passage is still suitable for initial recordkeeping, but it did not specify what to look at first when "only one side has feedback", nor did it require saving the location where the feedback appeared. Later supplementary notes filled in these gaps; the old paragraph is left unchanged to avoid retroactively inserting judgments that had not yet been formed at the time.

## 2024-03-20: A very quick but insufficient review

A follow-up review once took a very quick path: first checking that the final text was still present, then checking that a class had appeared near the global container. Neither check revealed any anomalies, and the record at one point stated "the content has not changed". This conclusion was later explicitly retracted.

What was retracted was not the two observations that "the text was still present" or "the class appeared". The former can still answer whether the user can see the content, and the latter can still help identify missing styles on the display side. What failed was combining them into a conclusion about the objects: that review did not save the original object from the caller, did not confirm which object was exposed on the mask side, and did not pinpoint the class to a specific node. Neither identical text nor the presence of a class can fill these gaps.

This review left behind an early-stop method that remains useful. When the content is completely invisible, there is no need to discuss object wrapping first; when the class is clearly absent from the display side, the review can also stay on the display path for the time being. Only once the content is visible and the class has been observed must the review proceed to obtain both objects. This avoids forcing a simple display issue into a content relationship issue.

```text
Next steps after the visual review
├─ Content not visible
│  └─ Stop at the container or display path, without assessing the caller node
├─ Content visible, class not observed
│  └─ Record where it is missing, then check the global display side
├─ Content visible, class observed
│  └─ Proceed to obtain the caller object and the mask-side object
└─ Only the final text is available
   └─ Do not document node relationships in this round
```

This branching does not require first determining where the fault belongs. It merely prevents "the page looks normal" from being misrecorded as "the content side has passed verification". If it is confirmed before the fixture that the supplied content does not exist, the review should still return to where the caller constructs the content; do not attribute the missing content to the global container, and do not continue using styling results to explain it.

## 2024-03-21: The fact that the objects differed was retained separately

The post-review addendum required turning "the objects are different" from a brief anomaly note into a formal branch. Earlier notes only considered whether the supplied content had disappeared: if the page still displayed text, it was easy to stop there. The addendum pointed out that when the caller can still obtain the original content, but the mask inspection point provides another content object, this relationship itself must be retained in the review results.

Subsequent records used three terms, without presenting them as a fixed implementation structure: caller-supplied content, content exposed on the mask side, the node with the global class. The first and second address the relationship between objects; the third addresses where the styling identifier is located. If all three are indiscriminately called content, the review results will collapse "what is displayed" and "where the class is" into a single statement.

| Observation point | Questions to record for this run | What this item alone cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Content passed in by the caller | Whether the caller can still retrieve that object | Whether the display side uses it directly |
| Content exposed by the mask side | Which object the inspection point actually receives | Whether the original object was deleted or rewritten |
| Node with the global class | Where the style identifier is | Whether the two content objects are the same |

The branches used after the review are shown below. Here, "stop" does not mean the issue has been resolved, but that when object evidence is insufficient, screenshots, text, or class placement must no longer be used to invent a complete explanation.

```text
Observations of retrieved content
├─ Both the passed-in content and the mask-side content can be retrieved
│  ├─ First record whether they are the same object
│  └─ Separately record where the global class is applied
├─ The objects on the two sides differ
│  ├─ Keep both objects in the record
│  ├─ Indicate where the class is actually applied
│  └─ Do not summarize this observation as "replacement"
├─ The objects on the two sides are the same
│  └─ If the appearance is still abnormal, then check the class and the display after attachment
└─ Only one of the two can be retrieved
   └─ Stop object-level attribution, add fixture observations
```

Different objects do not automatically mean that the caller's content was destroyed, moved, or rewritten. When the existing record lacks complete evidence from before and after attachment, this limitation cannot be bypassed. Conversely, finding that the objects are the same does not close out the appearance branch: the content may still be invisible, or the style identifier may still not appear at the expected display location.

## Old pre-release procedure left on the page

The following old procedure was reused in some regression notes, originally to quickly identify obvious display issues:

> After opening the global mask, confirm that the content is visible and the container has the global class; if these conditions are met, the content side passes. For validation messages, only capture the final displayed text.

This procedure is now deprecated, and the original text is retained. The first issue is that "content is visible" does not distinguish whether the page node and the caller's node are the same. The second issue is that saying the container has the class does not specify exactly where the class is applied. The third issue is that capturing only the final text conflates "no feedback" and "feedback exists but the text is different" into a single incomplete result.

It still has a very limited use: when the content is completely invisible, or the class is clearly missing, it can serve as a quick display-side check. But it cannot serve as the pass criterion for content objects, nor as the closure criterion for message issues. The old procedure has not been deleted because it explains why more information about object relationships and call results was later retained in the records, not to encourage continued reliance on it for judgments.

## Stopping points later added to the message branch

US validator message extension remains independent of the global mask check. Do not infer the cause of message issues from the global class, content objects, or the global container; do not treat differences in message text as evidence of mask wrapping either. The current evidence only supports observing the relationship between calls and visible feedback.

First separate successful calls from failed calls, then record whether each has visible feedback. When both produce feedback, record the text and where it appears; when only one produces feedback, first confirm whether the other call reaches the corresponding validator; when neither produces feedback, stop at observing the calls. If all you have is the final error text, you need to add one set of successful results and one set of failed results, and you cannot treat the wording itself as the complete observed behavior.

```text
US validator message extension
├─ Both success and failure have visible feedback
│  └─ Record the text and where it appears for each
├─ Only one has visible feedback
│  └─ First confirm whether the other reaches the corresponding validator
├─ Neither has visible feedback
│  └─ Stop at observing the calls, do not infer from the message text
└─ Only the final text was retained
   └─ Add one result each for a successful call and a failed call
```

The old note to "compare the final error wording" has not lost all its value. It applies when both sides have already been confirmed to produce feedback, allowing the displayed results to be compared; it does not apply to determining why a particular call produces no feedback, nor to confirming which internal object the message comes from. Do not introduce new attributions to factory, locale, or the message source here, as the existing observations do not support these claims.

## The distinction retained after the meeting

One review comment later retained in the page margin was: the mask and messages can share a page, but they should not share an attribution. This distinction is practical. For the global mask, inspect the object passed in, the object on the mask side, and where the global class is applied; for message issues, inspect the visible feedback from successful and failed calls separately. If either set of evidence is missing, it should not be filled in with results from the other.

Therefore, if the page only has a global content issue, the message branch on this page does not need to be followed; if only message feedback is abnormal, there is no need to look for the mask object first. Putting the two branches on one page is just a legacy navigation approach. When comparing, first confirm which entry point the observed behavior belongs to, then record the minimum observations for the corresponding branch.

## 2025-08-22: Current verification order

When investigating global mask content issues now, still start with fixture observations for `packages/overlays/test/DynamicGlobalLocal.test.js`. First confirm whether the passed-in content exists, then separately obtain the content object passed in by the caller, the content object exposed on the mask side, and the actual location where the global class is applied. The names dynamic, local, and global all appear at this entry point, and results from any other mode cannot be used in place of global mode.

If the content does not exist before the fixture, return to where the caller constructs the content; if the content is not visible, stay on the display path for now; if the class is missing, record where it is missing; if only one object can be obtained, stop attributing object identity. Once all three locations have been obtained, the current requirement is as follows: A global overlay retains the caller-supplied content while exposing a distinct wrapped contentNode carrying the global overlay class.

This sentence replaces the two old formulations, "global mode takes over the content" and "the content has not changed." It does not require attributing every visible anomaly to the wrapper: content missing before the fixture, content not visible, and the class missing still follow the preceding branches, respectively. Nor does it provide an internal attribution for the US validator message extension; on the message side, successful and failed calls still need to be observed separately.

## Adjacent issues not yet split off

`DynamicOverlayController` appears in the test entry point, but this page does not lay out the full relationship between dynamic mode and global content wrapping. If subsequent evidence clearly shows that the phenomenon is limited to dynamic mode, open a separate record; the only reminder retained here is that "dynamic results do not replace global results."

There is also a narrow gap on the message side: which layer stabilizes the visible results of the two calls, one successful and one failed. The existing material can only require separate observation; it cannot assign the boundaries of responsibility to the validator factory, locale, or message source.

## Appendix of old examples

### Old example: copy only the final DOM text

An early regression note once copied the final text and, because the text matched expectations, stated, "The content object is unchanged." This wording has been deprecated. The final text can still confirm the display result, but it cannot distinguish whether the content passed in by the caller and the content exposed on the overlay side are the same object. This old example is kept here to show why the object relationship can no longer be omitted.

### Old example: stop when the class is found

Another old example looked for the global class first and stopped once it found it. It is sensitive to missing styles but provides no information about content identity. If the class is on the wrapper node while the caller still retains the original content, the old example collapses the two layers into "content is normal." It can now serve only as a quick check of the visual branch.

### Old example: attribute message differences to the overlay

There was once a note that combined visible differences in validation messages with the global overlay and described them as a content-wrapping issue. Later, no evidence supported this classification. The two parts appear on the same page for historical reasons; the message side now checks only the respective visible results of successful and failed calls and does not accept attribution to the overlay branch.

# Decision on Outside-Click Policy and Property Reflection

This compatibility record placed two topics side by side in a way that was easy to misread: datepicker's outside-click policy and autocomplete reflection were recorded during the same closeout round, so early readers often followed the same search terms looking for a shared implementation. The verification added later did not merge them into a single chain of behavior, but instead clarified the original decision boundaries: one topic was traced back from the overlay controller entry point, and the other from the reflection results observed by the caller.

The old record can still be used to locate the material available at the time, but its search order must not be treated as documentation of the current interface. What follows preserves why changes were deferred at the time, which later checks were left incomplete, and which statements should no longer be extrapolated.

## The Decision on Record

At the time, the choice was not to adjust the local overlay's outside-click rules directly, nor to record autocomplete reflection as behavior already handled by `LocalOverlayController`. Three constraints were retained at closeout:

- datepicker's outside-click exception must first be tied to an actual usage path before deciding whether the issue concerns consumer configuration or the controller's scope.
- autocomplete reflection is recorded separately by caller entry point, version in use, and observed results; it does not inherit the conclusions about overlay merely because it appears alongside datepicker in the title.
- When the caller's environment cannot be accessed, the record can only say that verification was blocked, not that the behavior passed, and not that it failed.

The point of this decision was not to assert that the two topics were unrelated, but to avoid drawing overly broad conclusions from an incomplete picture of code adjacency. Time for the original compatibility work was limited, so narrowing the scope of changes first was more appropriate than betting on a shared entry point based on names alone.

## Where the Investigation Started

The issue name and call name in the old investigation record pointed to:

`packages/overlays/src/LocalOverlayController.js`

In the frozen revision, the file header directly confirmed only the following:

```js
import { render } from '@lion/core';
import { BaseOverlayController } from './BaseOverlayController.js';
```

These two items made `LocalOverlayController` a reasonable starting point for tracing back: the file uses `render` and also directly references `BaseOverlayController`. But they did not show where datepicker was created, where outside clicks were listened for, the conditions that triggered hiding, or exactly at which layer changes occurred between autocomplete's property and attribute.

The working hypotheses in early discussions went somewhat further: controller configuration might help determine the outside-click policy after overlay creation; reflection differences might simply be due to different caller entry points. Both statements remain in the historical record because they explain why the investigation took this direction at the time. No subsequent call snippets, test results, or actual DOM records accompanied them, so they were not elevated to interface commitments.

## Options on the Table

The approaches identifiable at the time were straightforward, but the strength of the evidence varied.

| Approach | Why it was considered | Why it was not adopted directly at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adjust outside-click behavior at the local overlay entry point | The filename was close to the search terms outside, click, overlay, and controller, so the path to a change looked short | It was unclear whether this entry point also served other overlays; if datepicker's exception became a shared rule, the regression scope could not be estimated |
| Have datepicker's consumer supply compatibility configuration | The exception could stay within the specific scenario without touching the shared controller first | No caller had yet been found that could reproduce the old path, and it had not been confirmed whether the old version depended on this configuration |
| Perform a caller-side walkthrough first, without changing existing behavior | This could bring the issue back from the filename to the actual entry point and actual results | It would not yield an immediate code change at closeout; if the environment was inaccessible, the walkthrough would also stall |

The final choice was a narrowed version of the third approach: verify the topics separately first, then decide whether to make any changes. This was not a finding of "no problem", but a refusal to substitute the path location of `LocalOverlayController.js` for call relationships. For datepicker, this meant leaving the general outside-click rules unchanged; for autocomplete, it meant not tying reflection differences to the overlay lifecycle.

## Why the Old Entry Point Remains

"Start with LocalOverlayController when looking at outside click" was once a useful order of work. The search terms could lead the investigation to a file that directly referenced the base controller, from which engineers could continue looking for configuration and usage sites. The error was in treating it as an ownership judgment: as though any issue mentioning outside click or controller should start with changes to that file.

The statement was later retained but narrowed. It still works as an entry point into the old investigation, but not as a way to decide who owns the final behavior. The file's direct adjacency to `BaseOverlayController` does not establish that there is a configuration point datepicker can override; likewise, the import of `render` does not establish that reflection occurs during rendering. The available material does not establish these relationships, and that absence cannot in turn be recast as assertions that "the base controller is not involved" or "rendering is necessarily involved".

The misunderstanding about autocomplete was slightly different. Its inclusion in the same compatibility train as datepicker shows only that the two items appeared side by side in the closeout work. If a caller reports differing results between a reflected property and an attribute, the caller's entry point and version should be retained first. Inspecting only the overlay file header cannot replace this step. Putting the two keywords on one page early on was intended to avoid losing leads, not to merge them into a single unit of change.

## The Two Verification Tracks Added Later

During subsequent maintenance, LION-206 was first recorded as `dependency_checked`, then changed to blocked later the same day. The blocker was that the account provided by the caller did not have permissions in that environment. This record did not establish where the outside-click policy was implemented, nor did it invalidate the original approach of starting the investigation from the controller; it only showed that verification of the caller's path had not been completed in that environment.

Therefore, the old decision's condition of "waiting for an actual consumer" was not met. The permissions issue cannot be interpreted as evidence for leaving datepicker as it is, much less as evidence that a change would break existing behavior. It merely left the observation that the caller was supposed to supply still missing.

The trail for LION-223, by contrast, first showed `caller_walkthrough`, then moved into `work_started`. This turned autocomplete reflection from one of the keywords listed together into a distinct track explicitly requiring caller follow-up. However, the available record provides no caller name, version in use, property value, or DOM comparison results. What can be confirmed is that verification had shifted toward actual usage; the record cannot be supplemented with claims that reflection had already been fixed, or that the difference was attributable to a particular browser or rendering point in time.

The status of the two tracks can be simplified into the following historical snapshot. The diagram is not a behavioral state machine, but only shows how the verification actions preserved in this record proceeded separately:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> entry
    state "Old investigation entry point" as entry
    state "LION-206: dependency_checked" as checked
    state "Blocked by permissions" as blocked
    state "LION-223: caller_walkthrough" as walkthrough
    state "LION-223: work_started" as started
    entry --> checked
    checked --> blocked
    entry --> walkthrough
    walkthrough --> started
```

The two branches in the diagram deliberately do not merge. The permissions block on LION-206 cannot replace the caller-side walkthrough for LION-223; work starting on LION-223 cannot fill in the results of datepicker's outside-click handling either. Drawing them as a single "verified" endpoint would go beyond the actions recorded on the cards.

## What This Decision Set Aside

The easiest option would have been to change outside-click behavior directly in the local controller. Its only advantage was that the entry point was close at hand: the old issue name, call name, and filename were adjacent to one another. The change was set aside not because it was necessarily infeasible, but because the scope of its impact had not been established. If datepicker was merely one of several overlay consumers, a change at the entry-point layer could remove other consumers' existing behavior; if autocomplete's reflection differences did not go through overlay at all, the change would not help the other track either.

The approach of keeping compatibility on the consumer side was likewise not declared complete. It appeared better able to preserve scenario boundaries, but depended on the actual caller, the entry-point version, and environment permissions. The later block on LION-206 illustrated precisely this cost: without an account that could access the environment, the outside-click policy could not be observed through the caller's path. Seeing the controller's two import statements in static code cannot supply that missing observation.

Therefore, "deferral" has a specific meaning in this record: do not change shared rules because of a group of adjacent search terms; do not attribute reflection differences that have not been tested in practice to overlay; when new material from callers becomes available, tie it back to each corresponding topic separately. It does not answer whether datepicker should hide or remain visible after a click outside it, nor which field autocomplete should reflect. At the time, the available material was not sufficient to make a final decision on those questions.

## Unresolved Relationships

The following gaps were not closed on the old page, and later readers should not fill in the answers from the title:

1. Whether datepicker's outside click is determined directly by `LocalOverlayController`.
2. Whether `BaseOverlayController` provides a configuration entry point that consumers can override.
3. Whether autocomplete reflection is linked to the timing of overlay creation, hiding, or destruction.
4. Whether the old caller still uses the same entry point as at the time.

These do not reopen a completed design choice. The limited decision already made was: do not expand the scope of changes to shared code while the relationships are unclear. Any additional material should provide actual call sites, the outside-click configuration passed in, or the DOM results before and after reflection; pasting the file header again will not narrow the gaps above.

datepicker's maintenance trail is still in LION-206, while the caller trail for autocomplete reflection is in LION-223. DOC-17 records an adjacent interface review and does not carry forward the assessments from these two histories. The page retains the original search approach at the end: look at the local controller first, then confirm whether the two topics really share an entry point. The first half can still help locate the old material, but the second half should now be treated as an open question, not an established fact.
