title: Registry Prerendering Migration Guide

versions.body:
# Registrar pre-render migration notes

This page follows the old migration sequence recorded during compatibility checks, covering two adjacent entry points: registrar pre-render state and guarded submit delegation. The old notes split them into two successive stages: the first prepares the registrar before form registration and rendering, and the second hands off to guarded submit delegation when a submit action occurs. The assessment at the time was that moving the earlier stage first would not change the submit stage, so the investigation started with registration order in the test suite rather than working backward from page callers.

### Notes on the old entry point

The original investigation looked at `FormRegistrationMixins.suite.js`. First find the form registration test cases, then read through the places where `new`, `registrars`, `portals`, `before`, `render`, and `update` appear. The point here is not to treat each term as a separate API, but to confirm whether the registrar has already been placed in the object used by the tests before render. The old notes treated "being able to access the registrar before render" as the main signal that the migration was complete; if a test only saw the result after update, this was usually attributed to test case order at the time, rather than the submit path.

Keep this sequence during the migration: first retrieve the registration object from the old registrar pre-render inspection entry point; then check the timing before and after it enters portals; then run the original render/update assertions; only then connect the submit action to guarded submit delegation. Do not remove the old registration assertions first, and do not backfill the submit result into the pre-render state. Both recorded stages must pass before the call sites can be switched to the new entry point. Limit the changes to this one suite initially; page-side replacements are not covered by these old notes.

### Cases still handled under the old assessment

If the registrar only appears after render, first go back to the locations of `new` and `before` and check whether the test object was created in advance. If the registration assertions pass but guarded submit delegation does not receive the submit action, the old procedure would continue by checking where delegation is connected; it would not change the registrar on that basis. If both fail, first restore the old registration call, then rerun the submit tests on their own; do not move both stages at once.

### Rollback

To roll back, undo the submit entry-point replacement and retain the original guarded submit delegation call shape; then restore the registrar to its old position before render and rerun the original registration tests. The old path is only restored when both the old pre-render assertions and the submit assertions return to their pre-migration results. If only one half recovers, leave the record at the failing stage and keep checking `FormRegistrationMixins.suite.js`; do not write it up as a completed compatibility migration.

Decision: keep two independent records. On the currency side, first record whether the issue can be reproduced consistently, then decide where to put the regression assertions; on the Space-key activation side, record only the user-visible results left by successful and failed calls, respectively. versions.body:
# Decision on Currency Parts and Space Activation

When this record was first written, only two names kept recurring in the wrap-up discussion: currency typed parts and Space-key activation. They were placed on the same compatibility release train, making it easy to assume that they should be addressed in the same implementation location, the same test, or even the same explanatory note. That was the easiest classification at the time, not a verified technical relationship.

The earlier draft made a conservative decision: document number-format part representation and keyboard activation separately. That decision remains in effect. Investigation of the currency issue starts with localized number formatting, while the issue with Space-key activation is examined in terms of what the user actually sees after a single invocation. The two tracks can appear side by side in release regression testing, but evidence from one cannot substitute for evidence from the other.

## Scope Recorded in the Initial Draft

`packages/localize/src/number/formatNumberToParts.js` is the local entry point currently available for the currency track. Four direct dependencies are visible at the top of the file:

```js
import { emptyStringWhenNumberNan } from './emptyStringWhenNumberNan.js';
import { getDecimalSeparator } from './getDecimalSeparator.js';
import { getGroupSeparator } from './getGroupSeparator.js';
import { getLocale } from './getLocale.js';
```

Early discussions treated these names as sufficient clues to explain typed parts. That assessment was later narrowed: they show the file's proximity to null handling, locales, decimal separators, and grouping separators; they do not directly establish the arrangement of parts in any particular user-visible output, nor do they identify where Space-key activation is handled. Continuing to infer the full behavior from these import statements would mistake navigation information for a conclusion.

The path's role here is therefore fixed as a starting point for review. When an anomaly occurs in currency typed parts, first use this file to check the local number-formatting logic, then compare the actual results observed with the regression samples. Do not pin down the implementation location based solely on the issue name or invocation name. This path does not provide evidence for Space-key activation unless a later review establishes an explicit connection.

## Later Notes

When LION-211 was created, it recorded a very specific observation: the output of currency typed parts could not be reproduced consistently. This was not a blanket judgment that "formatting is broken," nor was any particular separator confirmed to be incorrect. The issue was that output under the same name had not yet yielded samples that could be checked repeatedly.

The card subsequently underwent capacity_reviewed. After the review, the note "one point unconfirmed" remained; the work then moved from To Do to In Progress. This sequence changed how this record was handled: rather than waiting to guess all the part details first, the priority became deciding what the regression test should protect.

The record for LION-228 followed a different track. It required separately retaining the visible results of Space-key activation for one successful invocation and one failed invocation. The card later underwent documentation review. This did not establish that "all Space operations are now consistent," but rather a requirement to retain both results. Both samples are indispensable: if only the successful sample is retained, the failing usage pattern will disappear during later consolidation; if only the failed sample is retained, it will not show what the expected behavior originally looked like.

## Decisions Made This Time

The regression test for currency typed parts must assert user-visible results, not internal helper function names. LION-211 already made this explicit: add a repository regression test for "currency typed parts" that asserts user-visible results rather than internal helper function names. This choice does not presuppose which part entries will ultimately appear, nor does it turn `getGroupSeparator` or `getDecimalSeparator` into test names; it only establishes the output visible to consumers as what the test observes.

This approach has two direct consequences.

First, the portion that currently cannot be reproduced consistently remains unconfirmed. It cannot be filled in with a plausible-looking formatting example. If subsequent samples can be reproduced consistently, they should be added to the inputs and results of the same regression test; if the samples show that the original description mixed in another condition, that condition should also be listed separately, rather than compressing the two results into a single "compatible" label.

Second, the test is no longer responsible for attributing behavior to a particular implementation. It can protect user-visible results, but it cannot prove that a particular helper function is the sole cause. For this issue, source review and regression samples each have their own job: the former helps locate logic near number formatting, while the latter prevents the same externally visible results from drifting again.

The decision on Space-key activation is narrowed accordingly. The record must retain the visible results of both one successful invocation and one failed invocation; the regression test cannot contain only a generalized Space scenario. "Invocation" here retains the wording of the original card, without inventing element types, event paths, or browser differences that have not been provided. The available material only supports confirming that the results of the two usage patterns need to be retained side by side, not attributing the failure to bubbling, focus, delegation, or any specific control state.

## Approaches Compared During Review

What was actually on the table during review was not two complete implementations, but several approaches to structuring the records and tests.

| Approach | What it provides | Reason for not adopting it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Derive a typed parts test from formatting helper function names | Quickly produces an implementation-side assertion | User-visible results still cannot be reproduced consistently, and function names are not the consumer contract |
| Cover keyboard compatibility with one normal Space invocation | Provides one positive sample | Cannot retain the differences exposed by the failed invocation |
| Combine the two topics into one "legacy compatibility confirmed" note | Keeps the documentation short and easy to scan at release time | Would hide the unconfirmed portion of currency and incorrectly connect interaction results to formatting conclusions |
| Retain the results separately, then check them side by side during release regression testing | Keeps samples and verification entry points clear | Requires accepting different completion times for the two tracks |

The fourth approach was ultimately adopted. The trade-off is that the record will not provide a neat one-sentence overall status: currency may still be under review, while complete success and failure samples for Space can be recorded first. This fits the available material better than prematurely declaring the shared compatibility effort complete.

Another common way of filling in the gaps was explicitly rejected here: seeing `getLocale`, `getDecimalSeparator`, and `getGroupSeparator`, then listing all possible forms of the locale-sensitive part as expected results. Those dependency names are useful for orienting readers in the number-formatting context, not for replacing captured output. Without stable samples, the more detailed the list, the more likely it is to turn guesses into regression requirements.

Likewise, Space-key activation cannot be closed out with "keyboard support works correctly." Recording successful and failed invocations side by side requires readers to examine the visible results on both sides first, then judge whether they fall within the same behavioral boundary. The current material provides no basis for merging them.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> LocalObservation
    LocalObservation --> ReviewEntryPoint
    ReviewEntryPoint --> UserVisibleAssertions
    ReviewEntryPoint --> RetainUnconfirmedItems
```

The branch in the diagram is not an implementation flowchart. It only represents the handling sequence used in this record: after an observation is made, a local entry point can be found; after review, some information becomes user-visible assertions, while the rest remains unconfirmed. Both outcomes can coexist.

## Responsibility Boundaries Between the Two Tracks

The near-term work on the currency track is to add a repository regression test and have it express user-visible results. If reviewing `formatNumberToParts.js` reveals new connections around number formatting, record them as local findings, rather than retroactively presenting them as a completed compatibility guarantee. LION-211 remains the reference point for this issue.

The near-term work on the Space track is not to speculate about the failure mechanism, but to retain sufficiently identifiable results for both successful and failed invocations. LION-228 is the reference point for this portion. Completion of documentation review only means that this record has been checked, not that the failed invocation has disappeared or its cause has been identified.

DOC-22 discusses percent typed parts and ARIA reference DOM order. It is adjacent material on the same compatibility wrap-up release train as this page, but do not replace currency samples with percent conclusions, or use the DOM order of ARIA to explain Space-key activation. Similar names do not establish a shared regression boundary.

## Current Assessment

The decisions in this record can be reduced to three points: first establish a regression test for currency typed parts based on user-visible results; retain both successful and failed invocation results for Space-key activation; use the number-formatting source path only as an entry point for reviewing currency. Beyond that, the one case where output cannot be reproduced consistently remains unconfirmed, and no cause is assigned here to the differences in the failed invocation.

This is not setting the issues aside. It fixes the test formulation and documentation boundaries that can already be decided, while preventing implementation explanations not yet established from entering release messaging. If stable samples emerge later, they should be added under the corresponding topic, with an explanation of whether they change an unconfirmed item, a regression sample, or an existing local assessment.

Neither should endorse the other without its own observations.

## Changes Brought by This Round of Verification

LION-212 left behind `sample_attached`. The operation described on the card is: perform initial processing and reprocessing on `percent typed parts`, recording whether the content or diagnostics remain stable. Here, "reprocessing" is not meant to redefine the interface, but to expose state differences that appear only on the first pass through the entry point. The example itself should be kept in its original form, without rewriting observed diagnostics as passing results; this page has not yet frozen the example's specific numeric values or output text.

Therefore, the initial trial approach for number parts is to "keep existing consumer-readable results unchanged and add stability verification." At a minimum, retain the two processing runs side by side during verification, marking content changes and diagnostic changes separately; discuss whether a new public type marker is needed only when both can be explained. If the content is the same on the first and second runs but the diagnostics differ, compatibility still cannot be declared outright, because consumers may already be using the diagnostics themselves. If the content differs, pause interface expansion and first return to `formatNumberToParts.js` and its four direct dependencies to find the source of the difference.

This is a step narrower than the earlier idea of "finalizing a separate percent type right away": the new form remains a candidate, not a decision made in this round. This allows verification of what existing callers see before deciding whether to take on the migration cost. If a separate typed parts representation is ultimately still needed, limit the changes to percent-related results and the interface examples that use them, without also changing regular decimal, grouping separators, or locale selection.

The entry-point description for LION-229 is different: reproduce `ARIA reference DOM order` from the pre-call state and check whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. It provides no number parts results and does not say whether this file produces that ordering. The experiment here records only three things: the reference relationships visible before the call, the ordering of the referenced objects after completion, and whether any additional visible nodes or ordering changes appear. If the only finding is "there appears to be no change," the states before and after the call should still be retained to avoid presenting a lack of observed changes as an interface guarantee.

## How to Bring the Two Tracks Together

Both sets of results can be presented in the same compatibility review, but keep their result fields separate:

| What to observe | What to do first | What must not be done before verification passes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| percent typed parts | Perform initial processing and reprocessing on the same example, comparing content and diagnostics | Do not add a new public form or treat a single result as a stable contract |
| ARIA reference DOM order | Start from the pre-call state and record reference order and visible changes after completion | Do not attribute ordering changes to the number parts file |

This table is not the final compatibility matrix. It retains only the two observation actions for which this proposal already has entry points. The file path and helper adjacency on the percent track come from the `v_prev` navigation in `internal/LION`; there is no corresponding source-code mapping for the ARIA track, so no further call relationships will be inferred from file locations.

Only if both prove stable are there two possible next steps. The smaller option is to add an explicit regression test for repeated percent processing alongside the existing interface examples, and treat ARIA order as a separate caller-side check. The larger option is to release a separate percent typed representation and require known consumers to migrate; this option is worth taking only if the existing results truly cannot carry type information. Neither option should combine the changes on the grounds that they are "part of the same release round."

## Points of Contention Retained for Review

On the public-interface side, the concern is whether callers can consume public results reliably; on the module-implementation side, concrete changes are more likely to be demonstrated through a commit and test output; on the quality side, the version, environment, and CI node are needed to turn a single example observation into an acceptable regression. The three have different responsibilities for providing evidence; one screenshot or one local result cannot replace all of these judgments.

Three items remain undecided:

- whether the typed information for percent is already part of the existing results or requires a new form;
- which call entry point maintains ARIA reference order, and which visible changes are allowed after completion;
- how far each of the two verification tracks must progress in the compatibility train before the release can proceed.

When these questions lack supporting input material, keep them as candidates rather than stating them as finalized compatibility commitments. In particular, do not treat the adjacency of `formatNumberToParts.js` as directly establishing the responsibility boundary for ARIA.

## Withdrawal and Stop Points

If the two processing runs on the number track produce inconsistent results, existing consumers cannot read them, or changes in diagnostics cannot be explained, withdraw the new percent form, retain the original example and failure output, and stop expanding the interface. If the ARIA track shows additional visible changes before versus after completion, but there is insufficient material to establish that this is expected behavior, stop at comparing the pre-call and post-call states, without presenting it as an ordering fix.

Only after each track has its own verifiable results should the question of including them in the same release batch be revisited. Even if they ultimately enter together, retain two independent change notes: one focused on number parts and repeated processing, the other on reference order and visible changes.

# Date Validation and Button Visibility Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally started with a visible symptom: whether the date-related state on the page and the visibility state of a delegated button would change together after `calendar-day validation` completed. Early troubleshooting did not separate the two, and the common approach was to go straight back to `packages/calendar/src/utils/isSameDate.js` on seeing an issue name or call name. This entry point is still retained, but it can only help locate the local areas related to date comparison, not reconstruct the call chain from the path name or attribute `delegated button visibility` to the same function.

## Old Records, with the Original Assessment Retained

v1 initially recorded a working hypothesis: the two behaviors might occur in the same DOM update. At the time, the date state before the call was not consistently recorded, nor was the button's visibility captured separately. Therefore, "the button changed after validation completed" can only count as observed adjacent events, not as an established direct relationship between the two.

Returning from the issue name to the file, and then from the file to the issue name, used to be the easiest recovery action. Without reproduction inputs, this can only create a lookup loop: the file can be found, but the prior state of `calendar-day validation` has not been obtained; the button state can be seen, but it is unclear whether the change occurred before or after validation. This old action should not be treated as a successful recovery step, and its record remains here because later tracing may encounter the same path.

## Which Symptom to Check First

```text
Unexpected boundary behavior appears after date validation completes
├─ The date state itself is incorrect
│  ├─ The anomaly was already present before the call
│  │  └─ Stop at the input state, do not attribute it to the completion action yet
│  └─ Normal before the call, changed after completion
│     └─ Save the before-and-after states, then trace back to the date comparison entry point
└─ No observed change in the date state, but button visibility is incorrect
   ├─ The button change occurs at the same time as validation completes
   │  └─ Check the two time points separately, do not merge them into one conclusion
   └─ The button changes before validation completes or does not change
      └─ Pause the date path, record delegated button visibility separately
```

Here, a "change" needs an object that can be compared: at minimum, record the date values or display text before and after the call, along with whether the button exists and is visible at both time points. Writing only "validation failed" or "the button disappeared" is not enough, because it cannot distinguish whether the input was already at a boundary, the completion action changed the date display, or the button update happened first.

## calendar-day validation Branch

First keep the same date input fixed, then observe the state before the action. If the input has already crossed a month boundary, record the boundary position first; do not change the date, toggle visibility, and retrigger validation together in the same reproduction attempt. Otherwise, even if a result is observed, it will be impossible to tell which change triggered the visible difference.

```text
Before starting
├─ The date value or date text is already inconsistent
│  └─ Preserve the current state, stop assigning a cause; prepare the pre-call state again
└─ The date value and display text are consistent
   └─ Run validation once
      ├─ The date value changes after validation
      │  └─ Record the value, display text, and order of events, then check the adjacent references for isSameDate.js
      ├─ Only the display text changes after validation
      │  └─ Do not describe a display change as a date value change
      └─ Neither changes
         └─ Record "no visible change observed", do not write "did not execute"
```

If a retry is needed after the first reproduction attempt, restore the same pre-call state before performing the action a second time. Refreshing the page can be used to restore the test state, but the refresh itself discards the previous round's DOM state; without a before-and-after comparison after refreshing, "normal after refresh" cannot prove that the date comparison path has recovered. The same applies to repeated clicks: they may bypass the original timing, especially when the order of event delegation and DOM updates is unclear, and can only be labeled as another attempt.

The old reference to `isSameDate.js` came from tracing back through issue names and call names. During review, first confirm the direct references for that file in the corresponding code version, then decide whether it is on the validation branch. If the reference relationships have not been checked, troubleshooting can stop at the file entry point; do not present neighboring modules or button control logic as confirmed facts just to fill out the tree.

## delegated button visibility Branch

Button visibility anomalies require a separate prior state to be established. First record whether the button already exists and is visible before the action, then record its state between the start and end of date validation. If the button changes only after validation ends, save these two time points; if the button is already hidden before validation starts, date validation cannot be demonstrated as the trigger in this instance.

```text
Abnormal button state
├─ Already hidden before validation
│  └─ Stop classifying this occurrence as calendar-day validation
├─ Visible before validation, hidden after validation
│  └─ Save the date state and button state, continue checking the order of events
├─ Visible both before and after validation
│  └─ Record "delegated button visibility not reproduced", do not change the date assessment
└─ State changes with repeated clicks
   └─ Discard this round of comparison, restore the state before a single call and test again
```

When the button changes only under a particular delegated entry point, retain the description "entry-point-related" for now, and do not generalize it to mean that all buttons or all calendar actions are affected. This page does not currently have enough material to confirm a direct relationship between that entry point and `isSameDate.js`; only the tracing path and the two local symptoms that need to be compared can be confirmed.

## Environment and Timing Boundaries

When the same input produces different results in different browsers or with different mount timings, first record the environmental differences as reproduction conditions, and do not immediately choose one environment as the correct sample. In particular, distinguish the following: actions that occur before the control has completed DOM mounting, actions that occur after it has been mounted, and cases where the button is observed only after the date display has already updated. Without these time points, the order of `calendar-day validation` and `delegated button visibility` remains unknown.

If the issue appears only after a single call, retain the DOM state from before that call; if it appears only after the second call, do not combine the two results into one complete reproduction. Any normal result obtained through refreshing, remounting, or repeated clicks can only show that the recovery action changed the test state, not directly show that the original branch has been fixed.

## Stopping Conditions

Stop at the current branch in the following situations:

- There is no pre-call state, only a screenshot or written description after completion;
- Reference relationships can only be guessed from issue names, call names, or file paths;
- The date value, date display, and button state are all modified in the same action and cannot be separated;
- The same test state was not restored before retrying;
- The reproduction results only indicate "a change occurred", but do not identify what changed or in what order.

Stopping is not a conclusion. At this point, retain the symptoms, entry point, and missing comparison items, and start again from the pre-call state next time. Do not substitute "no change observed" for "checks not completed", and do not overwrite the failure state with one successful refresh.

The adjacent boundary month label records are kept at DOC-24; this page retains only the troubleshooting entry points where date boundaries and button visibility intersect. DOC-24 cannot replace the before-and-after state records on this page.

After the review for this version, the old direct attribution was not retained as a confirmed relationship. The file entry point, the two symptom types, the reproduction sequence, and the still-unconfirmed call adjacencies remain on the page; the page itself is still old troubleshooting material, not to be used as a new standardized operating guideline.

# Local Amount Parsing Decision Record

During this closeout, localized amount parsing was discussed as an input-component compatibility issue, but the only direct lead at hand was `packages/input-amount/test/parsers.test.js`. The file header also showed three dependencies:

```js
import { expect } from '@open-wc/testing';
import { localize } from '@lion/localize';
import { parseAmount } from '../src/parsers.js';
```

At the time, there were two ways to handle it. One was to treat `localize` appearing in the test as evidence that the parsing logic depended on the localization module, and to build out a compatibility conclusion directly from that judgment; the other was to leave it as a follow-up verification point, confirming only that the test placed the localization object and `parseAmount` in the same scenario, while leaving the specific parsing rules for subsequent review.

The latter was chosen. This choice neither assigns implementation ownership to the test file nor substitutes an import statement for checking actual inputs, return values, and error branches. Keep the compatibility discussion scoped to input amounts at this stage; if a later review finds that the issue comes from the localization package's configuration or state, split it out then.

What needs to be added now is not a longer test-case table, but a minimal example that can repeatedly point to the same place: once the localization settings are in the test, whether the handling of that example by `parseAmount` can still be rerun. The draft did not obtain the result of that run, so it did not state "can parse" as a conclusion.

Still open: the specific setup of `localize` in the test, and whether the parser is still called by other entry points.

# Locale Amount Parsing Decision Record

The first draft treated `packages/input-amount/test/parsers.test.js` as the shared entry point for reviewing amount parsing. That framing is still useful; however, a later review found that "entry point" could easily be read as "the localization package is responsible for parsing." What the file establishes is their co-location in the test: `@open-wc/testing` provides the assertion environment, `@lion/localize` is imported by the test, and `parseAmount` comes from `../src/parsers.js` in the same package. Seeing all three together does not, by itself, establish their respective runtime responsibilities.

The baseline record for LION-216 brought the issue back to a narrower request: select the shortest real example of locale amount parsing from the existing regression cases and check whether the result can be processed again. This is consistent with the direction of the first draft, but does not justify filling in input samples or results that were not recorded at the time. The card was later reassigned for follow-up because the original assignee switched to handling a production incident; that explains the gap in the record, but does not change the scope of the test file itself.

## Retaining the Earlier Assessment

The first draft's instruction to "look at `localize` and `parseAmount` together first" was an investigation sequence, not a judgment about module boundaries. It was chosen at the time because rechecking how the two were placed in the same test file cost less than changing the parser right away. This assessment is retained as context for revisiting the compatibility discussion from that time.

But the following statement is no longer a basis for the decision:

> The test imports a localization object, which means amount parsing should be handled by the localization layer.

It conflated test setup with responsibility boundaries. The statement was withdrawn after review. The only fact we can retain is that this test file places localization-related objects and `parseAmount` in the same test context; the parser's exact range of accepted inputs, format rules, and return behavior still need to be checked against the actual cases and implementation.

## Paths Considered at the Time

**Path A: Change the parser first.**

The apparent advantage was being able to respond quickly to "the old call failed." But the failure had not yet been narrowed down to a specific input or assertion, and changing `../src/parsers.js` directly would have bundled differences in localization setup, test fixtures, and parsing logic into a single change. Not adopted.

**Path B: Treat the localization package as a separate source of the issue.**

This path came up in discussion because `localize` was a visible import. But there was no material showing that the issue extended beyond the test scenario in input-amount. No separate conclusion on this yet; if later examples show changes in the setup stage itself, create a corresponding record then.

**Path C: Recheck using the shortest regression example and retain unconfirmed items.**

Adopted. This does not guarantee a full compatibility matrix. It only requires grounding the claim that "the old call failed" in a visible example: which localization settings the example used, what value was passed to `parseAmount`, and what processing result the assertion recorded. LION-216 is the navigation card for this review.

## Updated Decision

When reading or fixing locale amount parsing in subsequent work, start with `packages/input-amount/test/parsers.test.js` to find the existing test scenario, then revisit the implementation location of `parseAmount`; do not change boundaries between packages based solely on the import of `localize`. The test file is responsible for retaining the regression scenario, the parser is responsible for accepting the call used in that scenario, and the presence of `@lion/localize` shows that the scenario has localization-related context, but is not enough to determine the parsing rules.

Discussion related to end-of-month navigation is recorded separately in DOC-27. Both belong to the same compatibility wrap-up period, but the navigation issue cannot be used to establish how amount parsing is handled.

Still unconfirmed: the input for the shortest real example, its corresponding assertion, and the rerun output; and whether `localize` is only a setup condition in that test or contributes to the asserted result.

# Local Amount Parsing Decision Record

This record preserves the tradeoffs from a compatibility wrap-up, not a complete explanation of amount parsing rules. When it was first recorded, the discussion was driven by "the old call failed," and everyone initially focused on `packages/input-amount/test/parsers.test.js`. This file remains the most convenient lookup point, but at the time it also caused a very specific misreading: seeing `localize` imported led people to describe the responsibilities of the localization layer and the parser as if they were the same.

The relationship visible at the top of the file is actually very short:

```js
import { expect } from '@open-wc/testing';
import { localize } from '@lion/localize';
import { parseAmount } from '../src/parsers.js';
```

Based on this, the draft set the order of operations as follows: first find the shortest scenario in the existing tests, then decide whether to touch the parser. This order was not the problem; the problem was the explanation attached to it afterward. The draft described "a localization object and `parseAmount` appearing in the same test scenario" as if it meant "parsing is handled by the localization package." That is not a conclusion supported by the file.

## Scope of the Original Decision

What had to be chosen at the time was not the long-term architecture, but where to make the first change during the wrap-up.

One option was to directly modify `../src/parsers.js`. Proponents of this option believed that since the issue name pointed to locale amount parsing, changing the parser was closest to the symptom. The objections were also practical: there was no fixed input, expected result, or failure output, so the change would have to guess simultaneously at the localization setup, test fixtures, and parsing behavior. Even if a passing assertion were added, it would be difficult to know which layer had actually been fixed.

The other option was to first treat `@lion/localize` as an independent source of failure. This direction came from the test import, not from a confirmed runtime result. It could serve as a branch for follow-up investigation, but could not directly replace issue attribution. If it were prematurely designated as the source, the regression examples left in the input amount package would instead lose their context.

The draft therefore chose a third path: retain the test file as the verification entry point, without redefining module boundaries at that stage. Here, "entry point" only indicates where to start looking for existing scenarios; it does not mean that all relevant calls pass through the same file, nor that the test file contains the parsing implementation.

The draft's original intent should be understood as follows: first find an existing localized amount example, then see how `parseAmount` handles it. It did not obtain a rerun record for the actual example, so it did not, and should not, conclude that "a certain locale can definitely be parsed" or that "the old call has been restored."

## Counterexamples Retained Later

The most helpful counterexample during review was not a new format, but a counterexample to a way of reading the material.

- The presence of `localize` in the test imports does not mean that implementation ownership of `parseAmount` lies in the localization package.
- `parseAmount` being imported from `../src/parsers.js` shows that the test is meant to call that parser; it does not tell us which texts the parser accepts, nor how its return value is asserted.
- The presence of `expect` shows that a test assertion environment is used here; it likewise cannot replace a particular assertion itself.

All three points are ordinary enough, but they are sufficient to disprove the earlier approach of "assigning responsibility from a single import." For this record, the value of the counterexample is that it narrows the conclusion: co-occurrence in a test can guide a lookup, but cannot determine parsing semantics or package boundaries.

A passage from the earlier text was not deleted, to make it easier to understand how the discussion went off course at the time:

> Since the localization object is imported by the test, amount parsing should be handled by the localization layer, leaving the parser only a forwarding responsibility.

This passage was later rejected. It confused test setup with code responsibility and turned an unseen call flow into a conclusion. It was retained not so that the judgment would continue to be used, but because someone later returned to the test file from this passage and mistakenly assumed that the localization package was already the definite modification point. If this record is still cited, it should be read together with the correction in this section.

## Decision After Review

For LION-216, the decision is to continue using `packages/input-amount/test/parsers.test.js` as the first lookup entry for locale amount parsing; begin reading with the existing test scenario, then look back at the implementation location of `parseAmount`. During fixes or review, do not attribute the issue to `@lion/localize` merely because the file imports `localize`, and do not treat the test file as the implementation location for the parsing logic.

This decision is intentionally narrow. It constrains the starting point and attribution threshold for this investigation; it does not specify which locales a future parser should support, nor does it replace the specific test cases that should be retained. If someone needs to confirm whether a particular input can be processed, they must return to the relevant test content and parser implementation rather than extract a generalized answer from this page.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Test scenario lookup
    Test scenario lookup --> Modify parser directly: Not adopted
    Test scenario lookup --> Assign blame to localization separately: Not adopted
    Test scenario lookup --> Narrow-scope review: Adopted
    Narrow-scope review --> Specific example to be added
```

The baseline record for LION-216 provides a task formulation closer to the actual situation: select the shortest real example of locale amount parsing from the existing regressions and verify whether the result can still be processed again. This wording was adopted as the review objective because it avoids leaving "the old call failed" at the issue-name level. The card was subsequently taken over by someone else because the original handler moved on to a production incident; this change indicates that the review was not completed at the original pace, but provides no additional conclusion about parsing behavior.

There is another easily overlooked boundary here. "Shortest real example" does not mean casually constructing a piece of numeric text, nor does writing a locale name into an assertion count as coverage. It means the example in the existing regression that already carries the context of this issue. The current material does not retain that example's input, setup, or output, so this page cannot invent them. A follow-up review should keep all three together in the test or an adjacent record: what the localization setup was, what value was passed to `parseAmount`, and what processing result the assertion observed.

## Two Shortcuts That Were Rejected

**Change the implementation directly from the issue name.**

"Locale amount parsing" sounds like a parser problem, but an issue name is a navigation term, not a call stack. If `../src/parsers.js` were modified directly based on it during the wrap-up, the localization setup in the test would be skipped. This shortcut was rejected, not because the parser can never be changed, but because there was not enough material at the time to narrow the failure down to the parser.

**Elevate the import relationship to a dependency conclusion.**

The test file imports both `localize` and `parseAmount`, which is enough to remind the reviewer that the two objects need to be examined in the same scenario; it is not enough to show which object determines the result. This shortcut was also rejected. It had turned the discussion into "should the localization package be changed?" without first answering "what exactly is the existing example asserting?"

Rejecting these two shortcuts did not automatically turn the record into a complete fix plan. It merely ensures that subsequent people will not jump directly from a vague issue name or an import statement to the modification point.

## Previous Notation for Responsibility Boundaries

To prevent the same misreading from recurring, the boundaries are recorded by object rather than by a guessed root cause:

| Object | Role in This Record |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/input-amount/test/parsers.test.js` | Entry point for retaining or locating an existing regression scenario |
| `parseAmount` | Parser object called by the test; review `../src/parsers.js` for the specific behavior |
| `@lion/localize` | Localization-adjacent object in the test scenario; do not assign blame in advance based on the import relationship |
| LION-216 | Navigation cards pointing to review of the shortest real example |

This table is not the current owner table, nor does it assign any object to a particular team. It only addresses the object relationships most easily confused by this decision. The earlier wording that "the localization layer handles parsing" has been deprecated; if later evidence shows that the localization setup actually changed the parsing result, a new evidence-based judgment should be added rather than reinterpreting the old sentence as correct.

## Relationship to Adjacent Records

DOC-27 records the interface review for end-of-month navigation. The two documents belong to the same compatibility wrap-up and are therefore often found together; their objects cannot stand in for each other. Conclusions about month-end navigation cannot prove anything about amount-parsing input handling, and `localize` in the amount tests cannot explain the navigation path. When they need to be viewed side by side, treat them only as two clues from the same period.

Two types of field material are still missing: first, the specific assertion called the "shortest real example" in the existing regression; second, the runtime output from that example during review. The gap has not been closed. The final tradeoff retained here is: first locate the issue through the test scenario, then use the actual example to decide whether `parseAmount` or the localization setup needs adjustment; do not let the import list replace this step.

This decision has fallen behind subsequent changes to the code and tests, but it is still retained because it records the process of withdrawing from the incorrect attribution and returning to a narrow-scope lookup.

# Documentation Site Two-State Anomaly Postmortem

Early drafts described this anomaly as "The release notes were not updated along with the user-facing entry point." This sentence is retained here because the handling at the time did indeed start with the release notes; but it does not explain why the recovery page was available, nor why two pieces of content both referred to as the current revision could coexist.

Three kinds of things sit alongside one another in the documentation site: the user-facing entry points formed by docs and guide; the release notes; and the retirement action for handling expired content. Readers treat them as one body of content, but they may not change at the same time. The original record and the recovery page therefore did not replace each other.

## What Was Observed at the Time

The earliest observation was that the assistive technology path was inconsistent with the old record. The standard entry point did not immediately produce the same signal, so the initial wording was "The same object appears in two states," rather than a component failure or the entire documentation site being unavailable. This wording is narrow, but it matched the material available at the time.

After the anomaly appeared, the saved locator was:

`docs/adj-overlays/incidents/overlays-user-documentation-portal-two-states-for-one-object.md`

The original record retained the page state during the anomaly window. The recovery page retained the path through which content could later still be obtained. The recovery page made consumer contract available, but this does not mean that the change in DOM update timing has been explained. Early drafts placed recovery and cause next to each other, making it easy to read as "It has recovered, so the cause is known"; they are now separated, while the old wording remains.

## Records Added Later

| Record time | Material available at the time | Handling recorded |
|---|---|---|
| First observed | The user-facing entry point and the old record showed different states | Preserve the entry-point version; do not overwrite the original record |
| After retries stopped | The recovery page could continue to provide content | Keep the recovery result separate from the cause assessment |
| 2025-12-15 | Only a screenshot remained at the maintenance entry, and the original request corresponding to the retirement entry was not linked | Retain the screenshot as a locator; do not recreate the original request |
| 2025-12-18 | The two record versions were listed as independent event tracks | The documentation site retains its own overlays-documentation-portal and timeline |
| 2025-12-22 | The expiration action was still present, but the execution record immediately before the failure was not saved | Do not backfill the missing record as a particular execution |
| Same-day check | After switching to another account or workspace, the flow stopped upon reaching the retirement entry | This branch was not fully reproduced |

In the timeline, "recovery" only means that the user could later obtain content from the recovery page. It is not confirmation of the source of the two states. The initial draft did not distinguish these two terms, so the old wording below is not rewritten:

> The two states should have resulted from the current revision not being synchronized at the entry point; fixing the release notes first should be enough.

Later, no original request supporting this assessment was found. The maintenance entry retained only a screenshot, and the screenshot did not include the original request for the retirement entry. It is sufficient to show that the entry point was viewed, but cannot show when or from where each of the two revisions was written. The old assessment can still explain why the release notes were checked first at the time, but it cannot serve as a cause conclusion.

## Original Record, Recovery Page, and Retirement Action

The original record is not an ordinary backup of the expired notice; it preserves the state that had already been displayed during the anomaly window. The recovery page is not a revised version of the original record; it preserves the page path that the user could still access afterward. With both side by side, we can see only what once appeared and what could later be reached; we cannot infer the sequence of intermediate changes from their coexistence alone.

The release notes sit precisely between these two types of material, making them easy to mistake for the deciding source. That is how the old assessment was formed: since the wording differed, the wording difference was treated as the cause of the change. The existing material does not establish this step. docs, guide, the release notes, and the retirement action each have their own maintenance cadence, and any one appearing before or after another could create a temporary inconsistency; but without the original request and the execution record from before the failure, we cannot choose one of these possibilities.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant P as User Documentation Site
    participant O as Original Record
    participant R as Recovery Page
    participant X as Retirement Entry
    U->>P: Open the user-facing entry point
    P->>O: Preserve the state at the time of the anomaly
    P->>R: Provide the subsequent page path
    U->>X: Check the retirement action
    X-->>U: One path stops
    R-->>U: consumer contract available
```

The lines in the diagram only represent relationships among the material from that time, not a root-cause chain. The recovery page being available and the retirement entry stopping were once included in the same retelling, but there is no record directly linking these two things.

## Scope of Impact

The impact is limited to an inconsistency in how the same object is understood within the documentation site. People referring to the old record will see a state different from the current entry; people entering through the recovery page can continue to obtain usable content, but may not see the record from the time of the anomaly. Without complete request, input, or execution records, this description cannot be expanded to mean that all docs, all guide, or all users were affected.

Someone argued that the original record should be deleted after the recovery page became available, to prevent the documentation site from retaining two versions of the story at once. This was not done. Deleting the original record would leave the two-state situation represented only by a later one-sentence retelling; afterward, it would be impossible to tell when the old record existed, when the recovery page was available, or to review whether the release notes had actually ever been out of sync.

Another view was that as soon as different revisions were seen, expired content should be removed immediately. This was not done either. The retirement action still needs to be handled, but the old content in the anomaly window is itself part of the incident scene. Removing it first would instead eliminate the basis for determining whether the inconsistency came from the old record, the recovery page, or the retirement entry.

## Loose Ends from the Cards

LIONA-003 records the handoff arrangement after the maintenance entry was triggered: follow the action route from the maintenance entry to find the actual person taking over; remove groups that have already been taken offline from the new entry. A later record says that only a screenshot remained at the retirement entry, and the original request was not linked; the screenshot continues to be retained as a locator, not treated as a complete history.

LIONA-007 requires appending the recovery result to "overlays · User Documentation Portal The same object appears in two states", without overwriting the original failure window or object. The check that stopped at the retirement entry after switching to another account or workspace was also kept around this event, but the reproduction was not completed; it cannot therefore be attributed to the account, workspace, or retirement entry.

LIONA-011 saves the two record versions as independent event tracks and requires the documentation site to retain its own overlays-documentation-portal and timeline; the daily report contains links only. The card also records a gap: the expiration action exists, but the execution record before the failure was not saved.

LIONA-015 handles contacting the original owner before the retirement action expires and, if there is no response, closing out under the existing retirement action. It shows that expired content still has a handling entry; it does not show whether the unsaved execution took place, and certainly cannot connect the retirement action to the cause of the two states.

This postmortem still primarily follows the early page-side assessment. The release-note discrepancy, the availability of the recovery page, the existence of the screenshot, and the continued presence of the expiration action are evidence left from different stages; arranging them into a single cause would look more like a conclusion than the original assessment, but would be equally unsupported.

# Postmortem: The Documentation Site's Dual-State Anomaly

This page did not begin with a complete incident report. The first thing left behind was a very short field remark: the same object appeared to have two states in overlays · User Documentation Portal. Only later did someone break that sentence apart and discover that it mixed together the access entry point, the old record, the version notes, the recovery page, and the exit action.

The earliest remediation direction is still preserved near the beginning: the version notes had not been updated along with the access entry point, so fixing the version notes first should be enough. That was an old hypothesis, not a verified root cause. At the time, this hypothesis was sufficient to focus attention first on a visible fork, and it caused considerable confusion later. There were two sets of content referred to as the current revision within the documentation site, so readers naturally treated the newer wording as the answer; but the original record did not support the claim that "a change in the wording was the write source."

This page is outdated and easy to misread. It was not removed because the original record, the recovery page, and the exit action could still be encountered during documentation-site maintenance. If the early hypothesis were deleted until only a clean conclusion remained, it would actually be harder to see why two page states had been retained at the time.

## The Earlier Record, As It Was Written

The early draft did not have complete timestamps; it preserved only the sequence:

1. A state different from the old record was seen at the access entry points formed by docs and guide.
2. One entry point was still called the current revision, while the other gave a different revision.
3. Preserve the page content from when the save anomaly occurred, and stop retrying.
4. The recovery page subsequently made consumer contract usable.
5. DOM The change in update timing remained unanswered.

These five sentences seem simple, but they actually contain four different kinds of information. The first is an observation, the second is a presentation at the entry-point layer, the third is an on-site preservation action, the fourth is the result that the consuming side could still obtain the content later, and the fifth is an unresolved question. The old draft wrote them as a single paragraph, so readers could easily read "the recovery page is usable" as "we already know why the two states appeared."

At the time, the content seen through the assistive technology path differed from the old record. The ordinary entry point did not immediately produce the same signal, so the initial scope was not written as the entire documentation site being unavailable. The old draft's exact wording, "nothing was wrong with the ordinary entry point," should also be understood in this context: it meant that no similar difference was seen immediately; it did not mean that the ordinary entry point had undergone a complete check, and even less did it mean that all consumers received the same result.

The initial version-notes hypothesis must not be rewritten as the opposite conclusion. The evidence was insufficient to prove that the version notes were the cause, and equally insufficient to prove that they were definitely unrelated. They were simply the first location where a difference was seen. The value of retaining this old wording is that it explains why later records initially focused on revision, old links, and the recovery page.

## What Was Left Behind During the Anomaly

The saved locator has always been:

`docs/adj-overlays/incidents/overlays-user-documentation-portal-two-states-for-one-object.md`

The original record preserved the page state during the anomaly window. Here, "original" does not mean that it is more authoritative than the recovery page, nor that it saved the complete request. It simply was not overwritten after recovery. This matters to anyone who needs to revisit the initial discrepancy; if only the recovery page remained, there would be no way to know which two states the documentation site had once presented simultaneously.

The recovery page preserves something else: consumers were later able to continue accessing the content. Having a usable consumer contract on the recovery page is a practical outcome, not an explanatory one. The recovery page provides no record of which locations wrote each of the two revision values, nor does it explain why the assistive technology path differs from the old record. It did not replace the original record, and the original record did not prevent the recovery page from continuing to serve as an access point.

The exit action is a third type of material. It deals with content on the documentation site that may already be outdated. When the anomaly occurred, the old content could be both something awaiting handling and part of the observed state. Removing the old content immediately would make the documentation site look orderly again, but would lose the display state at the time of the anomaly. The early decision was not to overwrite the original record, and to retain the exit action separately. This was not because the old content had been confirmed to be correct, but because the relationship between the two states was not yet known.

The release notes sit between these materials and are the easiest to misread as a final verdict. They describe what the page displayed at a particular point in time, and do not automatically indicate whether docs, guide, the recovery page, or the exit entry point changed in sync. The old draft collapsed this distinction, leading to the hasty conclusion that "fixing the release notes first would be enough".

## Why there were no further retries

Stopping repeated attempts to open the same entry point during the incident was not a successful recovery. Repeated retries did not yield any new original material, and would only keep showing pages that might already have changed afterward. If every read were treated as the initial state, it would become harder to distinguish the original record from the post-recovery state.

What was retained was therefore the version from that time, not a series of pages refreshed later. This choice also had a cost: the materials do not preserve exact timestamps between the first occurrence and recovery, making it impossible to construct a minute-by-minute timeline. Later readers can only confirm the relative sequence: inconsistent observations came first, then the entry-point state was saved and retries stopped, and afterward the recovery page was recorded as usable.

The early record did not clearly state what "stopping" meant, and someone later misread it as meaning that the entry point had been isolated. There is no material supporting that. It only means that repeatedly opening the page was no longer being used as a troubleshooting method at that time. The documentation site continued to exist, and the original record and recovery page continued to coexist.

Another easily overlooked gap is DOM update timing. The draft only says "unknown", without providing trigger conditions, a page version, or the complete input. This unknown cannot be resolved by the recovery page being usable. Nor can it be used to assert a change at a particular implementation layer, because the retained materials contain no records from that layer.

## Later addenda and earlier assessments

The later maintenance records did not have the original request. The LIONA-003 addendum on the maintenance entry point states that the original request associated with the exit entry point was not attached, and only a screenshot remained. The screenshot is still useful: it can point people to the vicinity of the entry point being viewed at the time. It has no request context, cannot reconstruct a complete operation, and certainly cannot explain the relationship between the writes of the current revision values at the two locations.

The choice for handling this card was to retain the screenshot, not recreate the original request. This choice makes the review look incomplete, but it is closer to the material available at the time than reconstructing a smooth history from the screenshot. This gap provided no additional support for the earlier assessment about the release notes; it remained only a working hypothesis.

LIONA-011 later listed the two versions of the record as separate event timelines, the resource site continued to retain its own overlays-documentation-portal and timeline, and the daily report included only links. A single link in the daily report therefore cannot replace the original record, nor can it be used to piece together the full sequence of events. Keeping the two versions of the record separate does not mean they have been proven to be two independent root causes; it simply prevents the recovery result from overwriting the anomaly window.

The same set of supplementary notes also pointed out that the expiration action was still in place, but the execution record for the run before the failure had not been saved. This also leaves a gap in the history of the exit action. We can tell that the resource site once had arrangements for handling expiration, but we cannot tell whether that unsaved execution took place before or after the anomaly, much less describe it as the action that caused the dual states.

LIONA-007 required appending the recovery result to "overlays · User Documentation Portal Two states for the same object", without overwriting the original failure window or object. "Appending" is more accurate than "fixing" here: the recovery page provides a subsequent result, not deletions or modifications to the original record.

There is another check recorded near this card: after switching to another account or workspace, the flow stopped at the exit entry point. This observation cannot be directly conflated with the initial anomaly. Without a complete reproduction, it is impossible to determine whether the stop was due to the account, the workspace, the exit entry point, or simply that the check itself did not continue. Placing it after the assessment about the release notes in the old draft would create a causal chain that does not exist.

LIONA-015 only concerned contacting the original owner before the exit action expired, and wrapping up using the existing exit action if there was no reply. It leaves an entry point for handling expired content, not a conclusion from the investigation into the cause. Whether the original owner replied, when the action was carried out, and whether it was carried out at all cannot be inferred from this arrangement as established facts.

## Retained Old Passages

The passage below comes from an early draft and has not been rewritten to reflect the later way of reading the records:

> assistive technology differs from the old records. The revision at the current entry point has diverged. Check the release notes first. The recovery page works, DOM update timing is unknown.

Not every sentence in this passage was refuted by later material; the problem is that, when compressed together, they look as though they already form an explanation. Reading it against the available records, the first sentence is an observation made at the time, the second is the entry point's state, the third is a direction for investigation, the fourth is a recovery result, and only the fifth is the question that could not be answered at the time.

Another old claim that has been retained is: "As long as the release notes are updated, the two states will converge." There is no corresponding execution record for this claim. Proving "convergence" would require, at a minimum, observing both entry points again under the same conditions; the material contains no retained record of such an observation. The release notes may be where readers first see the difference, but they cannot be treated as the source of the change on that basis alone.

Another earlier proposal argued that, since the recovery page was already usable, the original record should be removed to prevent the documentation site from presenting two different accounts. It was not adopted. The original record is precisely where the anomaly window can still be reviewed. Deleting it would turn "the same object appearing in two states" into a secondhand account unsupported by page states, and would also lead later readers to mistakenly believe that the recovery page had always been the only entry point.

The earlier proposal's call to "immediately clean up outdated content" was not followed either. There was indeed an exit action for the outdated content, but the cleanup action and the anomaly record are not the same issue. The old content had value as contemporaneous evidence during the anomaly window; the documentation site could only first let the recovery page continue serving consumers, then keep the exit action as a separate maintenance item.

## Relationships among the materials at the time

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Consumer
    participant P as User Documentation Site
    participant O as Original Record
    participant R as Recovery Page
    participant V as Release Notes
    participant X as Exit Entry Point
    U->>P: Open the usage entry point
    P->>O: Retain the state at the time of the anomaly
    P->>V: Display one revision
    P->>R: Provide the subsequent page path
    U->>X: Verify the exit action
    X-->>U: One path stops
    R-->>U: consumer contract is usable
```

This is not a causal diagram. The fact that the original record, release notes, recovery page, and exit entry point appeared around the same documentation site at the same time does not mean that any two of them were driven by the same action. There is also no line from the recovery page to the release notes in the diagram, because the materials show no such relationship; it has likewise not been confirmed that stopping the exit entry point would change the recovery page or the original record.

The early account treated these locations as a single chain, and the later supplementary notes did not contain enough information to replace it with another complete chain. All that can be done is to separate the purposes of the different pieces of material: the original record preserves the states that were observed, the recovery page retains a usable path, screenshots preserve location information, the exit action preserves the handling plan, and the release notes preserve the text that readers saw at the time.

## The impact did not expand

This anomaly affected how the same object was understood within the documentation site. People referring to the old record would see a different state from the one at the current entry point; people entering through the recovery page could continue to access usable content, but would not necessarily know that the record from the time of the anomaly was still there. This description does not say that the two groups of consumers necessarily got opposite results, nor does it say that all access paths were affected.

No complete request was available initially, and no execution records from before the failure were obtained later either. Therefore, the impact cannot be described as a problem affecting all docs, all guide content, or all consumers. The regular entry point did not immediately show the same kind of discrepancy, but that is also not enough to state that the regular entry point was already functioning normally. Both can only be retained as local observations.

The scope of impact appears conservative not because the anomaly was unimportant, but because the documentation site's objects were made up of multiple types of content to begin with. The usage entry point, release notes, and the handling of outdated content can show different states in adjacent locations. Without a shared change record for them, expanding local differences into a unified event would allow page-side speculation to go beyond the materials.

The usable state of the consumer contract provided by the recovery page must likewise be understood only in this context: it eased the blockage preventing consumers from continuing to retrieve content, but it did not close out the historical dual-state issue. The original record remains, there is still no complete answer to how the two current revision entries once coexisted, and the change in DOM update timing has not been explained either.

## Differences between the two maintenance approaches

The initial handling focused on the version notes. Because this was the most obvious point of divergence, people could immediately decide to "fix the wording first". This approach gave the documentation site an apparently actionable direction, but it also conflated the presentation location with the source of the change.

Subsequent maintenance did not recast this judgment as a new, definitive root cause, but instead kept the materials separately:

- The entry-point version at the time of the anomaly remains in the original record;
- The usable result from the recovery page is retained as an appended record;
- When the original request for the maintenance entry point is missing, screenshots are used only to locate it;
- When there is no pre-failure execution record for an expiration action, no execution is retroactively fabricated;
- When the switching path on which the exit entry point stopped working has not been reproduced, no cause is assigned.

These items do not constitute a complete remediation plan, nor do they share a common completion time. They come from different stages and guard against different common misreadings: treating screenshots as requests, treating recovery as an explanation, treating an expiration action as an execution that has already occurred, and treating an unfinished path as the cause.

The documentation site therefore still looks somewhat disorganized. The original record, recovery page, version notes, and exit actions have not been consolidated into a single narrative. For people who need to look up the history, this untidiness is more useful than a retrospectively unified account; for those who only want to find the current entry point, it is also more likely to lead to misreadings. This is precisely why this page has long not been treated as the current guide.

## Gaps that remain unfilled

The exact time when the discrepancy first appeared was not preserved. For when the recovery page first became usable, only the relative sequence is known, with no complete timestamp that can be checked. There are no original requests to trace the respective sources of the revision writes at the two locations. The record of that execution before the failure was not preserved, so no link can be drawn between the expiration action and the anomaly.

The assistive technology observations remain limited to a particular setting. They have not been extended into a conclusion about all access conditions. The existing page records do not answer why DOM update timing changed; the recovery page being usable, screenshots existing, or exit actions still being present have not provided a substitute for that missing answer.
