# Alternative Route Proposal for the Docs Site

This proposal records an approach to organizing the docs site that was not adopted. The original idea was narrow in scope: separate the records around overlays-documentation-portal from the existing categorization and list them separately as `release regression`, while the material still in use would continue to be found via `browser compatibility`. At the time, this looked like a categorization change that could keep the material better separated, but it was not adopted as part of the docs site's official plan.

The initial draft included the sentence "The exit points are different." It did not make clear what it referred to and could easily give the impression that the correspondence between the old and new pages had already been confirmed. It is retained here only as the assessment at the time: different ending points appeared in the same material, which is not enough to infer two stable, interchangeable usage paths.

The candidate proposal would have done three things:

- List `release regression` separately on the docs site so it would not get lost in the explanation of `browser compatibility`;
- Make `package entrypoint` the reference point for this branch;
- Return to the old entry point on withdrawal, rather than leaving the candidate category as a semi-public second route.

The second item was the first to hit a blocker in review. The draft did not list the active callers of `package entrypoint`, so there was no way to tell whether it was just a name in the material or a location readers would actually reach. Adding it to the navigation would make the docs site appear to offer another usable entry point; the available records did not support that promise.

Another objection concerned how to exit. The subsequent LIONA-009 record says `release_classified`, with this explanation retained: the internal results include the current result, while the ordinary entry point corresponding to the exit entry point does not. This observation is enough to reject the assumption that "both sides can fall back in the same way after the split," but it does not fully explain why the ordinary entry point is missing. This record therefore does not single out the docs-site page, package entry point, or upstream release as the cause.

After the sample was attached on LIONA-013, the checks became more specific: retain the two states of overlays-documentation-portal in the order they occurred, and first confirm whether they refer to the same object. The earlier draft treated the "dual states" as evidence for the split; that was premature. Adjacent states and similar names are no substitute for checking object identity. This correction also explains why the candidate route was not pursued as a trial: even the boundaries of the material to be organized were not yet settled.

## Not Adopting the Proposal

The recommendation is not to establish `release regression` as a separate docs-site route, and not to put `package entrypoint` in user-facing navigation. `browser compatibility` remains the category under which this batch of old material can be found; `release regression` stays in this record as a candidate name that was compared at the time but not adopted. This is not a judgment that the latter has no value; it keeps an unverified reference point from taking on the role of a docs-site entry point.

Withdrawal here does not mean reverting a change that has already gone live; it means stopping work on the split. The stop conditions have already been met: the callers of the candidate entry point are unconfirmed, and the ordinary entry point cannot be aligned with the internal results. With these two gaps, adding more pages, tags, or explanations would only increase readers' mistaken impression that the route is usable.

The original draft's question, "Should only the old entry point be restored on withdrawal?", is retained, but its meaning needs correcting. There is no new entry point being implemented, so there is no restoration action to execute. What needs to be answered first is what kind of docs-site link the old entry point refers to, and whether it can still cover the material that needs to be found. This proposal does not resolve that question.

## If the Discussion Is Reopened

Before reopening the discussion, fill in the following three gaps rather than simply copying the category names from this proposal:

1. Whether `package entrypoint` has any actual callers, and whether those callers need docs-site navigation;
2. Whether the two states of overlays-documentation-portal are indeed before-and-after records of the same object;
3. Whether the relationship between the "current result" and the missing ordinary entry point in LIONA-009 can be reproduced as a clear observation without broadening the scope of the explanation.

As long as any of the three remains unanswered, the candidate proposal can only remain historical material and should not be relabeled as a migration or release plan. Even if the objects are confirmed to be the same in the future, whether the split makes it easier for readers to find the right material still needs to be assessed separately; confirming object identity is not itself a reason to adopt the proposal.

The material is still at `docs/adj-overlays/proposals/rejected-overlays-user-documentation-portal-route.md`. LIONA-009 and LIONA-013 can be used to review their respective state records; this page only preserves this route comparison, the objections, and the reasons for not proceeding.

# Package Integration Cache State: Trade-off Decision

This record began with a very narrow judgment: don't rebuild the environment at hand just to get a clean set of package integration results. During later review, the dispute was not whether the cache had value, but what would remain from the original state for comparison if a new recovery result overwrote the "current revision".

Two kinds of material were always in play. The first is the current revision left near the existing entry points; these records show the package set actually obtained later. The second is the original failure window; it may not be complete, but it preserves the order in which the problem appeared. Mixing the two kinds of material into a rerun result makes the page look cleaner, but the decision loses its provenance.

The earliest draft stated the choice too simply: retain the current revision; do not rebuild the environment. At the time, there was not enough material to show where recovered records should be placed, and the gap in the middle had not been handled. This wording remains above because it explains why the old window was not simply cleared later.

## The Two Options Considered at the Time

| Approach | What it provides | What it gives up |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild an environment and then cross-check | A package set organized from scratch, making it easier to continue trying it out | The original failure window would be covered by the new execution order, making it impossible to tell whether a difference came from the cache, recovery, or the environment itself |
| Keep the current revision and append alongside the original state | The original records and later results can be read side by side | The entry point is less tidy, and missing intermediate records do not appear automatically |

We did not choose the compromise of rebuilding first and then bringing the old records back. Once old records are detached from their original window and only final values remain on the page, the brought-back content cannot replace the ordering from that time. LIONB-005 later separately flagged cases where the current revision was inconsistent with the page chronology; this is exactly why the page's final values are treated only as corroborating evidence, rather than used to overwrite the original window.

A standing objection was that retaining only one real path makes the sample too narrow to represent every package entrypoint. That objection is valid. Here, the single path was not elevated into a cross-package conclusion; it was used only as the starting point for continued recording. The comparisons in LIONB-001 and the work that began afterward all stayed within this scope.

## Decision

Keep the original state; do not rebuild the environment for this comparison; from the recovery point onward, append only the first current revision. Save the recovery result alongside the original failure window; it must not replace any objects or the order in the original window. Do not include subsequent summaries in this round's assessment.

This does not treat the cache as a long-term retention mechanism. The cache is simply the form taken by material that already existed for this round. The items to verify are the version combination for `localize-package-integration` and consumer-side integration; if rebuilding the environment changes either one, record the new result separately rather than writing it as a continuation of the original state.

The restriction to "first" later became an explicit procedure in LIONB-012: after recovery, retrieve the first current revision; defer the later summaries. This restriction prevents the sequence of post-recovery records from gradually crowding out the original window. It also makes clear, when someone next needs to expand the scope, which entry marks the start of the new material.

## Handling Added After Review

LIONB-003 pointed out that intermediate records were missing. The decision was not to fabricate a continuous timeline, but to leave the gap blank and have whoever can modify the test fixtures handle the follow-up alignment. The blank itself cannot prove that nothing changed during that period; it only means that this trade-off record has no intermediate material to put there.

LIONB-010 require the recovery result to be appended beside the trade-off recorded on this page. When appending it, retain the original failure window and its objects; do not write "recovery succeeded" as an explanation for the original phenomenon. Recovery only says what was obtained later; it does not automatically answer why the difference appeared at the time.

Read this page in two separate layers: the original window is for reconstructing the package integration state at the time; the first current revision after recovery is for confirming which new starting point the recovery action produced. If the two are the same, that does not prove the preceding sequence was irrelevant; if they differ, this page alone cannot attribute the cause to the cache.

## Scope Not Expanded

This round did not bring all consumer integrations into scope, nor treat the page's final values as the sole basis. The intermediate package-integration window still has gaps; the available material supports preserving it as-is, not filling in content for it.

Related entry points: LIONB-001, LIONB-003, LIONB-005, LIONB-010, LIONB-012. When earlier localized experiments need to be reviewed, DOC-33 still retains the original notes; its relationship to this page is to provide an adjacent observation, not to change the trade-off already made here.

# Caller cache and state preservation: trade-off decision

This page originally recorded a trade-off, not a caching strategy: preserve the current revision in the caller's environment for validate-client-integration, rather than rebuild the environment to get a cleaner reproduction. The original reasoning was that rebuilding would produce a different state, which could not replace the state the user had already seen.

That reasoning remains here because it explains why the environment was not immediately torn down. It also had a consequence that was later overlooked: if "preserve the state" is read as "the state is already sufficient," cached results will be mistaken for confirmation, and exit actions can easily be mistaken for completion. The old passages have not been rewritten here to address that gap.

## The two options originally considered

One option was to keep examining call samples on the current revision, using the cache as a copy to make handoff easier. The other was to rebuild the environment, then write up the issue based on the post-rebuild results. The former preserved the state at the time, but required later readers to distinguish between the original state and the cache; the latter looked easier to document, but would change what was being compared.

The first option was chosen at the time. The objection remained: using the cache made it easier to continue integration testing and for someone other than the author to take over. That benefit was not denied here; the inference that "the cache can replace the original state" was not accepted. No decision had been made at the time on whether backing out meant restoring the old entry point or making a broader restoration.

The old decision therefore had a narrow scope: it preserved the state observed during one round of integration testing. It was not an assessment of cache reliability, the shared test environment, or all caller versions. The later problems fell precisely in those unresolved areas.

## Notes later appended to the decision

During work on LIONC-009, the last adopter confirmed only who was on duty, not the version in use. This feedback conflicted with the earlier leaning that "the cache is already sufficient for handoff": having someone present does not mean the version the adopter is using has been confirmed. No conclusion about the version can be drawn from this; confirmation has to come from the original state and the adopter's records.

LIONC-010 was blocked when the shared test environment was temporarily unavailable, then returned to the backlog because its timing did not line up with the release window. At the end of the window, the active entry point still had the old value. The record does not attribute that old value to a single cause; both the old cache and the old task remain candidates. The earlier wording that treated the environment issue as a brief pause was no longer adequate in light of this observation, but the original text is retained rather than pretending the distinction was already clear at the time.

LIONC-009 also noted that validate-client-integration did not match the rollback state of the exit actions. A partial restoration cannot be recorded as full completion on that basis. The original statement, "preserve the state first," provided no order of operations for this. That is also why this page was retained later but is not suitable as the basis for a new process.

## Updated decision

The decision to preserve the current revision stands, but only to support comparison with the original state. The cache must be preserved alongside the original state; cleaned-up green results must not overwrite the original state. If the adopter has not confirmed the version in use, the version in the cache must not be marked as confirmed either.

Exit actions must be checked separately. If the active entry point still has the old value after the window ends, first record the old value and when it occurred. Do not directly attribute it to the cache, or treat a return to the backlog as a completed rollback. If the shared test environment is unavailable, this integration-testing effort may be stopped; do not use that as a reason to rebuild the environment to create a substitute for the original state.

When retracing this trade-off, anyone other than the author should check against the release and operations checklist item by item; if any item is missing, stop at that gap. LIONC-011 records this handoff requirement, not a comprehensive revision of the old decision.

Still unresolved are the scope of restoring the old entry point, whether the old value came from the cache or the old task, and when the cache is sufficient to support handoff. The available records do not settle these questions. Supplying definite answers would hide the gap between this page's original choice and the later exit problems.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Mismatch Postmortem

During the maintenance window, the result shown by the public entry point did not match the original plan. The first observation was a mismatch in results, not a fault that had already been pinpointed; the execution records left at the time could only show which operations had been performed during the window, not directly explain why this result occurred.

Before the window began, the plan was still understood to assume that the old entry point was usable. The old entry point's state, the maintenance actions, and the expected display had not been recorded separately up front, so once the mismatch appeared, the sequence could only be recalled by working backward from the result already seen. This gap affected later judgments: the records could show that the plan and the entry point's display were inconsistent, but not at which step they diverged.

When the mismatch appeared, the response initially focused on the entry point itself, based on the assumption that temporarily restoring the old entry point would let users return to the original maintenance path. This temporarily brought the visible result back to an acceptable state and preserved an entry point that could be withdrawn. The restoration action itself left no evidence that the cause had been resolved, so "restoration" could only be treated as an outcome of the immediate response, not as evidence that the fault had been located.

The sequence at the time can be reconstructed in three stages: first, the maintenance plan still used the old entry point as its reference; then, the entry point's display diverged from the plan and checks of the visible result began; finally, temporary restoration made the entry point usable again. The existing records do not provide the full operational details between these stages, nor do they say whether the mismatch persisted during the window. The restoration time should be retained as the time restoration occurred, not backfilled as the time the cause was identified.

When the record was supplemented later, it emerged that the actual impact had not been documented separately at the outset. What could be confirmed was that the maintenance plan and the entry point's display were inconsistent, and people relying on that entry point to determine the state at the time would receive conflicting information. It could not be confirmed how many users had already acted on the incorrect result, and there were not enough records to establish impact outside the window. The impact assessment should stop at what was observed; broader effects on users should not be inferred from the abnormal entry point display.

The coordinator was responsible at the time for keeping the restoration actions and the original execution records in the same place, to avoid a situation next time where only "restored" is visible and the incident context cannot be found. The added controls were: record actual impact when the mismatch appears; retain the original execution records during restoration; and, when using the old entry point for restoration, note that it can still be withdrawn. These measures addressed the records and the withdrawal conditions, not the cause itself.

The earlier judgment is retained here: after the temporary restoration, the team for a time understood the problem as an incomplete switchover involving the old entry point. That judgment fit the mismatch seen at the time, so it was not removed from the record; it was not a root-cause conclusion, however. The available material still does not establish at which step the original plan and the visible result diverged, or whether the mismatch will recur in the same way in the next maintenance window. Subsequent records should continue to keep the observed result, the restoration action, and the unconfirmed cause separate.

"In-package check complete" is not enough. At minimum, wait until the package-side check and the monorepo regression point in the same direction before proceeding with closure; if they disagree, keep the release item open.

# Common Questions About Maintaining Public Entry Points

This page was originally treated as a quick-reference for public entry points. Several terms have actually been used interchangeably all along: an in-package test path, a candidate path, and an external-facing entry point are not the same object. The old version is still being looked up, so the revised answers are placed under the original wording without erasing the earlier conclusions.

## What can the existing localize-number entry prove?

The earliest reference was `packages/localize/test/number/getFractionDigits.test.js`. It is in the localize package and supports the claim that there is an in-package check here related to the number of decimal places; it cannot by itself prove that a particular localize-number path is already a public entry point, nor can it stand in for a package probe. The old version overstated what the file location and the name of a single test established.

Accordingly, when the question is whether the existing entry is usable, first treat the candidate path and the package probe as two separate things. Without the original execution record, don't work backward from the old FAQ to infer that a run already took place; this remains logged as unconfirmed.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing a candidate path?

"Whoever proposes it withdraws it" was the old rule; it remains here because it once made withdrawal look like an individual action. If a candidate path involves a legacy-browser exception, the proposer may initiate the change but cannot strike out the exception alone; the owner taking it over and the rollback decision must both be left on record. The old version did not spell out this relationship, making it easy to read withdrawal as nothing more than deleting one path line.

## Under what conditions can it be closed?

The closure wording currently in use is: "A release item closes only after its package probe and the monorepo regression path agree, with any legacy-browser exception linked to an owner and rollback decision."

Here, "agree" does not mean that passing either one is sufficient. The package-side probe and the monorepo regression path must produce consistent results; the legacy-browser exception is not allowed by default either, but must be linked to an owner and a rollback decision. The localize test mentioned above is at most a possible lead for the probe; it cannot replace these two determinations.

Regarding where the original execution record is stored, this page does not provide an answer. A single-variable rerun note is recorded under DOC-50, but that note cannot substitute for the missing record.

The old entry point must not be deleted outright in this round; if later adjustments are approved, the record must clearly state its status as an entry point that can be withdrawn.

versions.body:
# Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

This decision did not treat "public entry point maintenance" as a unified cleanup effort. At the start of the discussion, the team faced a narrower question: form-registration was still being provided to consumers through the current entry point, but there was no existing consensus on whether the entry point arrangement within the package should be changed during the adjustment window. The entry point appears to be a team-level concern, but its impact can only be assessed through specific consumer paths and package-level changes; the meeting therefore began by discussing retention and adjustment separately.

The initial draft stated the conclusion as "keep the current entry point for now". That sentence was sufficient at the time to prevent unsupported changes, but it was also easy to read as meaning that the entry point had been permanently frozen. Following review, this wording needs to be made more precise: what is being retained in this round is the currently known compatibility state, not a long-term commitment to the future form of the entry point. New adjustments may still be proposed later; the adjustment window itself simply cannot be treated as grounds for approval.

## Two Approaches Compared

**Retain the current form-registration entry point.**

This approach is straightforward: consumers continue to obtain the existing behavior through the current entry point, and the team does not rewrite it before the evidence has been laid out. This is not without cost. The entry point will continue to support historical usage patterns, and package-level cleanup may also need to be delayed. That cost, however, is visible; consumers do not have to bear both entry point changes and behavior changes in an adjustment with no clearly defined scope.

**Change the entry point arrangement during the adjustment window.**

The window is valuable only if the change has already been narrowed to a package-level scope that can be explained. The proposer must be able to provide a reproducible consumer path and connect that path to evidence in the repository. Only then can reviewers determine whether the change really preserves downstream behavior, rather than merely seeing a change in the entry point name or the location of local tests.

The meeting did not reject the adjustment window as a tool. What it rejected was a different argument: since there is a window, the public entry point can be changed first, and consumers can report problems afterward. That sequence leaves the compatibility costs to downstream consumers and also fails to explain when or how the old entry point should be restored. Changes to the public entry point should start with known consumers, not with the desired directory layout.

## Decisions in This Round

1. The current form-registration entry point will be retained and will not be replaced as part of this round's adjustment window.
2. Approve only the smallest package-level change covered by the existing materials; entry point cleanup beyond that scope is left for later discussion.
3. Every approved adjustment must document the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry point available for rollback. Here, "available for rollback" is not an abstract promise, but means that reviewers must be able to tell whether the old entry point can still be restored.
4. Entry point names, test file locations, and call names can serve as leads for tracing back, but they cannot by themselves establish compatibility.

Together, these four points constitute this round's decision. Saying only "retain it" would omit the conditions for later adjustments; saying only "adjustments are allowed" would erase the protection the current entry point provides for downstream consumers. The decision is not centered on choosing a better-looking entry point, but on first defining the scope of changes the team can confirm.

The order of assessment used in the meeting is retained below:

> Compatibility decisions begin with a reproducible consumer path and repository evidence, then narrow to the smallest package-level change that preserves downstream behavior.

This statement does not require a broad audit every time. It requires anyone proposing a specific adjustment to first describe a reproducible consumer path, then use repository evidence to narrow the impact to the smallest package-level change. When the evidence is insufficient, the conclusion can go no further than retaining the current entry point; unconfirmed aspects cannot be presented as routine maintenance within the window.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Reproducible consumer path] --> B[Repository evidence]
  B --> C[Smallest package-level change]
  C --> D{Downstream behavior can be preserved}
  D -->|Can be confirmed| E[Approve this local adjustment]
  D -->|Not confirmed| F[Retain the current entry point]
  E --> G[Record actual impact, coordinator, and old entry point]
```

In the diagram, "can be confirmed" does not mean that a particular file exists, nor that a search for a call name returned a result. It means the path, the evidence, and the proposed change can be assessed together. Conversely, failing to find a complete path does not automatically mean that the entry point has no consumers; it only means that this review cannot yet approve a larger change.

## Leads Retained from the Review

This review traced back through `packages/field/test-suites/FormRegistrationMixins.suite.js` and the related call names. This was the entry point lead actually used at the time, and it is useful for bringing the discussion back to the local behavior of form-registration. That does not make the file the permanent home of the public entry point, nor should it be used as a substitute for a consumer path. Entry point maintenance covers more than a single test suite; the test location only answers where tracing starts, and cannot by itself answer which consumers will be affected.

The initial draft did not make this clear enough, making it easy to mistake "there is a lead in the code" for "the impact has been verified". That lead is now retained, while its role is limited to a starting point for review. Anyone citing this record to propose an adjustment should continue from that lead to fill in the consumer path and package-level impact, rather than request removal of the old entry point based solely on the filename.

The notes on the relevant call relationships are stored in DOC-01; the code-reading details in that material are not repeated here. For this decision, what matters is that the material can help investigate the connection between the entry point and the calls, rather than turning call names into grounds for approving every change.

## Handling the Old Entry Point

"Retaining the old entry point" has two levels of meaning in this discussion. The first is keeping the current entry point available to avoid passing unconfirmed changes directly on to consumers. The second is that, even if later local adjustments are approved, the old entry point must be explicitly recorded as a rollback option. Reviewers need to know whether it is still there, who coordinates it, and which part of the approved adjustment would be affected by restoring it.

No deletion date has been set here, and there is no promise that the old entry point will exist forever. That is because those conclusions require material on consumer paths and actual impact; this round has not filled those gaps with assumed facts. Retaining the entry point does not mean doing no cleanup, but refusing to make deletion a fait accompli before the scope of impact has been narrowed.

The coordinator's role is also limited to this matter: coordinating the actual impact of entry point changes and the status of the old entry point. It is not a generic maintenance title. When no coordinator is listed in the record, reviewers cannot tell who will confirm consumer issues during the adjustment, nor who should take ownership of a decision to roll back the entry point, so the adjustment should not automatically be approved just because it falls within the window.

## Matters Not Decided in This Round

The still-unconfirmed matters are retained here, rather than glossed over with "retain the current entry point":

- Which specific usage patterns the current consumer paths can cover;
- If a package-level adjustment is proposed, which downstream behaviors must be explained individually when it is proposed;
- Under what conditions the old entry point is considered still restorable after an approved adjustment;
- Whether there is a separate opportunity for entry point maintenance outside the adjustment window.

These questions cannot be resolved simply by adding a generic checklist. They determine, respectively, whether the impact can be explained, whether the scope of approval can be narrowed, whether rollback is genuinely available, and whether future discussions should still proceed within the same window. Without new material, no unified migration plan should be inferred from this decision, nor should consumers not listed be included in the scope of impact.

## Objections and Reasons for Retaining the Entry Point

The review retained a reasonable concern: continuing to retain the current entry point would make adjustments within the package look slower than they actually are. This concern is valid, especially when entry point maintenance and local changes arise at the same time, as waiting for path documentation will delay cleanup. But the cost on the other side is harder to reverse: if the public entry point changes first and consumers discover behavior differences only later, the team can only restore the old entry point or continue supporting both arrangements after the change has already spread.

Therefore, this round did not use "more thorough adjustments" as the priority criterion, but used "the smallest change that can already be substantiated" as the boundary. This choice does not deny the benefits of cleanup, but puts downstream behavior ahead of the shape of the public entry point. The objections should still be reviewed again alongside any adjustments proposed later; once the consumer paths and repository evidence are specific enough, the cost of retaining the current entry point should also be reassessed.

Finally, keeping the decision reversible does not mean allowing arbitrary trial changes. Keeping the old entry point available for rollback is a constraint on approved local adjustments: the person proposing the change must explain the status of the old entry point before making the change, the coordinator must be able to confirm the actual impact, and only then can reviewers judge whether restoration is still possible. Without these three elements, the adjustment window can only remain an option under discussion.

This round's conclusion goes no further: the current entry point is retained; local adjustments may be proposed, but approval covers only the smallest package-level scope that can connect consumer paths, repository evidence, and downstream behavior.
